speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Yesterday, when urged to introduce back-to-work legislation which would end the damaging postal strike now in its second week, the Prime Minister replied that Mr. Parrot, head of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers, "made it clear that, if legislated back to work, he would disobey the order." Therefore the Prime Minister said he was "at a loss to know what would advance negotiations for a settlement in this area." subsubtopic: POSTAL STRIKE-QUERY RESPECTING GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister who is aware, I assume, or must be aware of the direct and indirect costs of the postal strike or mail strike. After all, the government was extremely

July 7, 1981
Oral Questions
eloquent about these costs in 1978. Reliable estimates to date are that between 1,000 and 1,500 small businesses will go bankrupt each week, that 6,000 to 9,000 jobs will be lost each week, that the direct mail business people will lose some several millions of dollars every day that the strike goes on, not to mention those who are dependent on mailed cheques, and also the costs to government of lost revenues. Can the Prime Minister therefore confirm to this House whether, in fact, the statements of the President of the Treasury Board yesterday, to the effect that the government is prepared to see this strike go on all summer, are government policy?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: POSTAL STRIKE-QUERY RESPECTING GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member does not ignore that any strike anywhere is bound to hurt someone. A strike against the government is more serious than other strikes. The basic question is: do we recognize the right to strike of public service unions or not? If one recognizes the right to strike, whether it be in the private or public sector, the way the strike operates is by effecting damage on one or other of the parties, and sometimes on third parties. I have not heard the Conservative party come out clearly and suggest that we abolish the right to strike. If they do, that will be more consistent with the position which they have been taking in the past few days.

subsubtopic: POSTAL STRIKE-QUERY RESPECTING GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, the Conservative party has not heard the government indicate that it even cares whether these people go back to work. The government's position, I take it, as again expressed by the Prime Minister, is that the government would prefer a settlement at the bargaining table. That has been his position all along. At the same time the government has clearly indicated that it refuses, in any way, shape or form, to modify its offer. That suggests one interpretation, and one only, that there is only one settlement acceptable to the government, and that is the government's offer itself. Can the Prime Minister, in face of that, therefore indicate to this House and to Canadians how we would expect to get such a settlement without legislation?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member is quite wrong in the premise of his question. We have not said we would not discuss or we would not modify. We have said that that should be done at the bargaining table. Surely, if it is to be done at all, the other parties should come to the bargaining table and begin bargaining.
Some hon Members: Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, we have this strike because for three days there was hard bargaining at the bargaining table, and the government's negotiators
were given a mandate not to move one penny, one inch or one jot on a clause. The only credible way in which one can interpret the Prime Minister's answer to this House is to assume that the Prime Minister and the government in fact, are planning an initiative which they have not yet announced. Therefore my question to the government is this: does the government, in fact, intend to adjourn this House before the strike is settled?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we do not know when the strike will be settled. We do know that the House leaders are talking about adjournment days. The opposition House leader mentioned possibly next Friday. I believe the House leaders are discussing matters now. Therefore the two events will happen, one before the other, or the other before the one, depending on whether-
Oh, oh!
It might happen simultaneously, depending on whether the CUPW union negotiators want to come down and sit at the table.

Madam Speaker, I would like to address my supplementary question to the Prime Minister. After the rather gobbledygook answer he gave to the previous question, perhaps he could give some clarification to the rather ridiculous proposition that he put forward yesterday, in terms of the fact that legislation was not contemplated because Mr. Parrot would not obey any law which was brought before Parliament and passed by Parliament. It was not bad enough that the Prime Minister said that, and I thought that maybe it was a joke on his part, but the Liberal headquarters in Toronto are now giving that answer to people who are phoning in to ask why the government is not taking any action. The answer given is that it is because Mr. Parrot will not obey any law which is passed by Parliament. I want to ask the Prime Minister whether it is government policy that it will not bring in any legislation until Mr. Parrot is satisfied with the law which will be passed by Parliament.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, if the hon. member refers to my answer yesterday, he will see that I was pointing out the rather, I believe, unsustainable position of the union leaders. Mr. Parrot, on the one hand, does not want to sit down and negotiate, which, as the hon. member's colleague argues, should lead us to want to legislate; but on the other hand Mr. Parrot says he would not obey the legislation, if I understand him to be reported correctly.
Throw him in jail.

Therefore I think that this indicates that the union leadership is somewhat inconsistent with its logic. I wish the hon. member would attack that question rather than the position that I explained in the House yesterday.

July 7, 1981

Madam Speaker, the position of the Prime Minister is completely irrelevant to the whole issue of whether Parliament should have the right to legislate as it sees fit and as is appropriate under the circumstances. What the Prime Minister has done, in effect, is to give Mr. Parrot a veto over whether Parliament is going to act and to take its responsibility.
Negotiations between CUPW and the government are paralysed. The Prime Minister seems to be paralysed by a fear of Mr. Parrot. I want to ask if he has no compassion for the average citizen of this country who is bearing the brunt of the postal strike, and will, if we listen to the President of the Treasury Board, bear the brunt over the course of the summer until Parliament is reconvened, at least until next fall. Has he no compassion? Will he not give an undertaking that, unless there is some movement forward before Parliament adjourns, he will take legislative action? We on this side are prepared to stand and take our responsibility and to stay here until the matter is resolved.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I wish the hon. member opposite had not referred to the fear of the government of union leaders. If my recollection is exact, it was during the 1980 election that the party opposite, when it formed the government, settled with the LCUC at an unconscionably high rate. It did that because it was afraid either of the union leaders or the electorate.

subsubtopic: EL SALVADOR-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT POSITION ON HOLDING OF ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and it concerns the question in El Salvador which is continuing to do damage to the people there. Recent reports in The Globe and Mail indicate that the people in the elite, who one would think would support the present junta, are saying, and I will read a small paragraph quoting a person interviewed there as follows:
He regards elections for a constituent assembly, scheduled for next March, as "a gimmick" to cement the Christian Democrats' hold on power. "Nobody else is going to campaign," he says. "They'll be killed the first day."
In light of this situation, I wonder if the minister is now prepared to reconsider his position regarding conditions in El Salvador.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: EL SALVADOR-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT POSITION ON HOLDING OF ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member quotes some people from the press who were interviewed in El Salvador. There are many people interviewed by the press about the situation there. It is not our role to pass judgment on the daily events in that country in that respect. Having profound faith in
Presence in Gallery
democracy, we believe the best way to resolve the problem of that country is through free elections.

subtopic: METHODS TO ENSURE RETURN OF PEACE
METHODS TO ENSURE RETURN OF PEACE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my second question would be along a similar line. I, too, believe that the question should be solved in a democratic way if that is possible. It would also seem, and again I take my information from journalists going into the country, that now the peasants likewise see no possibility that there can be free elections. I would ask the minister again if he is prepared to look at other ways in which the problem can be faced, so that peace can return to that land.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: METHODS TO ENSURE RETURN OF PEACE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, our interest is certainly in peace, and in a political settlement. We retain an open mind on the best way in the future to proceed toward that. We have not lost our confidence that the democratic process and the process of free elections can bring about a resolution to the problems in El Salvador.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I should like to ask the minister if he would be prepared to go and talk to his counterparts in the different countries neighbouring El Salvador, the ministers of external affairs for Mexico, Venezuela, Cuba and Nicaragua. subtopic: NEGOTIATION OF AGREEMENT WITH PROVINCE OF ALBERTA
NEGOTIATION OF AGREEMENT WITH PROVINCE OF ALBERTA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. It is very clear that the lack of an agreement with the province of Alberta on energy policy as well as the many other aspects of the Liberal energy program, including the Fina purchase, increased imports, etc., have resulted in a large outflow of capital of approximately $10 billion over a one-year period, with a consequent increase in interest rates of at least 3 per cent to 4 per cent.
Is the government conducting any studies on the cost of this 3 per cent to 4 per cent increase in interest rates to the Canadian economy, whether it is to small businessmen, home owners, large business, governments themselves, all of whom must pay these high rates directly as a result of the Liberal energy program, and are these costs related in any way against any possible benefits that might be gained from these protracted negotiations?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: NEGOTIATION OF AGREEMENT WITH PROVINCE OF ALBERTA
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member's question seems more rhetorical than real. I have no way of challenging these figures which he brings forward. They are of a statistical nature. He asked if studies are being done. I am sure that if the hon. member sends me the basis of his calculations, I could have them verified. But in so far as the issue itself is concerned, the hon. member knows that there have been meetings, even quite recently, between officials and ministers of the government of Alberta and the Government of Canada, and both sides have stated that they very much want to reach a settlement satisfactory to both sides.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER ENTER NEGOTIATIONS
REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER ENTER NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am very surprised that the government is not conducting any studies on the cost of high interest rates to the Canadian economy-

subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER ENTER NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: I did not say that.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER ENTER NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: -because it is clear, according to many observers, that these are as a result of the National Energy Program. The three to four percentage point increase in interest rates, the deadlock with the province of Alberta, the high imports of oil, the loss of 40 per cent of Canada's drilling rigs, are all the result of the failure of the minister of energy to reach an agreement with the province of Alberta. The cost to Canadians in the form of these high interest rates, the $6 billion increase in tax that has taken place, plus the lost opportunities, is immense. Will the Prime Minister now accept his responsibility, replace the minister of energy in the negotiations and take part himself directly with the Premier of Alberta, and try to reach some resolution to this stalemate after 16 months of failure?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER ENTER NEGOTIATIONS

subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER ENTER NEGOTIATIONS

speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Minister of National Defence

4,000	miles of coastline both on the Atlantic and on the Pacific coasts. We try as much as possible to centralize our equipment and resources in locations where most incidents happen. Everyone knows that we try to station most of our equipment on the west coast for spring fishing and we do the same in north eastern Canada at the time of the seal hunt. However, with the resources and the equipment now at our disposal, we make every effort to save lives, and I believe that rescue operations were most satisfactory in the case of the Prinsendam, for instance. subtopic: ADULT OCCUPATIONAL TRAINING ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND

speechtext: The House resumed, from Monday, July 6, consideration of the motion of Mr. Axworthy that Bill C-67, to amend the Adult Occupational Training Act (No. 2), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

subtopic: ADULT OCCUPATIONAL TRAINING ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, once again I should like to reiterate what I was saying last night when the
House adjourned. I think the minister and his departmental officials are to be complimented for bringing forward Bill C-67.
As I said last night, under the present legislation there is little incentive for an individual to enter an apprenticeship or training program in the adult area because, as things presently stand, people who are unemployed can go on unemployment insurance and remain on it and they have absolutely no incentive to go for retraining or training.
I have a couple of suggestions for the minister regarding the legislation. Hopefully he will be able to incorporate them in the legislation. It provides an extra $25 per week above the unemployment insurance figure which an individual would draw if he goes into adult occupational training. I find this provision to be particularly good because some incentive is offered to an individual to go into training.
One area amended by the bill which I feel is good but does not go quite far enough is that extra benefits will be given to those people entering employment training in certain skilled areas or trades. Currently these are targeted at tool and die makers, welders and boilermakers, these very specialized areas designated by the governor in council. Somehow a mechanism must be put in place in the various regions of our large country for an advisory committee appointed by the Department of Manpower and Immigration to evaluate at a very local level the kinds of occupational training which are essential for an area.
Nowhere do we see in the legislation as a skilled area the requirements of the hotel service industry or the food service industry. Yet these industries in certain localities within our great country are hard-pressed to find trained employees. Employees working in the hotel and food service industries need intense training, perhaps not for as lengthy a period but certainly as intense as the training of a tool and die maker.
The legislation itself is narrowing down too quickly and zeroing in on only those areas where in the past shortages have occurred to such an extent that employers have gone to the Department of Employment and Immigration and requested permission to seek workers elsewhere in other countries and bring them in as landed immigrants.
I am particularly pleased that the legislation will lift the one-year ceiling on government assistance to trainees. We all know that many programs go beyond one year; some last two years and some even three. Also I am pleased that the legislation will abolish the requirement that trainees must be out of school for at least a year. The current legislation is very discriminatory. It really causes a great deal of hardship for young people who are not functioning academically in the school system and want to enter training programs. The only training programs being offered are those supported by manpower assistance. Manpower arranges the training place in junior colleges and technical schools. These young people have actually been denied admittance into the schools. This is being addressed in the legislation; again the minister should be complimented. Previously if a course was not offered in Canada and students had to go outside the country for train-
July 7, 1981

ing, the government offered no support. Now it has recognized this need and included it in the bill.
The government is primarily amending this piece of legislation so that the department of manpower will be able to sign contracts. They then propose to sign training contracts, but they aim primarily at unions with the thinking, of course, being that unions are in a position to know their manpower requirements. If unions do the training, then those unions in the specialized trades in particular will be more prone to accept a trainee into its ranks and, therefore, offer employment.
One area which I think is not being addressed clearly enough is the employment of native people. If one goes to certain bands, particularly the ones I am familiar with in northeastern Alberta, one will find that the need and requirements of the band may be something very nebulous. An official sitting in Ottawa might not consider that training programs are needed. I direct the attention of the House to basic life skills training programs. Many of the enlightened bands in northeastern Alberta have attempted to train their men and women in basic life skills.
These programs cover a myriad of topics which we in urban society take for granted and expect everyone to understand. I am talking about banking, immunization programs, public health programs for children which we take for granted, and basic housekeeping. After years of living in shacks without running water admittance is suddenly gained to more modern housing. It takes skills to go into these homes and run them in a way which we all take for granted since we were raised in those kinds of homes. I am afraid the minister is missing something here by not putting into place legislation to sign contracts with the unions for training programs and contracts with various bands throughout the country on the basis of a suitable training program to develop the skills necessary to survive in our Canadian communities. I would like to see the minister add a clause to this legislation which would clearly indicate the intention of this government, through the Department of Manpower, to address this very serious problem.
Another aspect of the legislation which is before us that I thought was particularly good is that dealing with the negotiation of fixed rate training allowances with employers. There was no such provision in the old legislation. In other words, you can negotiate fixed rate training allowances with employers.
Although the legislation is long overdue, and although it is good, I must point out to the minister the sense of futility which is felt not only by the people in the Department of Manpower but by members on this side of the House in respect to there being no forecasting facility to pinpoint areas which need employment incentives in skilled labour training.
I would like to expand on this point. Legislation is brought in to deal with the retraining and training of people for employment opportunities which are developing in the country. Later on another minister will introduce legislation, for exam-
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2 pie the National Energy Program, which will destroy an industry to the point where the people who hold skilled jobs move to another country. I am talking about the drilling industry. It takes two to three years to train good drillers, good floor men and good derrick men in the drilling industry. But what will happen when the government finally comes to its senses and enters into an energy agreement with the producing provinces? All the skilled labour will have left the industry, along with the rigs. Each rig employs 20 to 30 people and each is like a small factory.
I would like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that one megaproject in northeastern Alberta, and I am referring to the Alsands plant in Fort McMurray and the Cold Lake plant, causes a secondary spin-off into the Ontario economy which will affect training programs geared for Ontario. Can you see the inconsistencies, Mr. Speaker? On the one hand is a minister who brings forward what I consider to be long overdue and good legislation, while on the other we have a minister who brings in legislation which counteracts the first.
One $10 billion plant in northeastern Alberta will create $800 million in business for Ontario's iron and steel industry. What will happen when the iron and steel industry slows down, as it is doing today? Trained employees will be lost. When the plant starts up again it will have to fill the positions which have been vacated in order to meet the capacity and requirements of the megaprojects. Training will have to be targeted in these areas. This cannot be done in a vacuum, nor can it be done under the present legislation without there being a coordination of legislation.
Bill C-67 does not complement what is happening as a result of the National Energy Program. That same $10 billion plant will create $370 million in business opportunities for Ontario's metal working industry. As a matter of fact, one should double these figures since there are two plants which have investors waiting to spend money to the tune of $20 billion to $22 billion. It has been forecast that there will be five or six plants like these developing in northeastern Alberta.
That same plant will create $325 million for the Ontario transportation industry. Today the transportation industry is sagging. It is losing its trained employees who are moving to other parts of Canada where they feel they can find a job. Some of these people are taking retraining. Imagine trained men in the industries in Ontario and Quebec leaving their jobs and taking retraining because the market has sagged. Legislation is now brought forward which would enable these men to be retrained for another job.
Once an energy agreement is reached with the producing provinces, the activity in central Canada will increase and then we must retrain other people to fill the jobs which have been vacated. This concept staggers the imagination. There is no apparent co-ordination between government departments, at least co-ordinating the legislation, so that we are not duplicating or wasting our resources, which in the main is our manpower.

July 7, 1981
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
One plant creates $740 million for other manufacturers and processors in Ontario. That is a secondary spin-off. It creates $370 million for Ontario financial enterprises and $750 million for the Ontario trade and service sector. Those are the kinds of matters we have to address. It is just too bad that there is no co-ordination. This means $1.8 billion in extra Ontario household income which, in turn, generates again.
As I said, the legislation before us is good. I am sorry it does not go further. I am sorry that the government does not seem to be co-ordinating and trying to bind together the legislation so that there is a complete understanding. I do not know what ministers do at these cabinet meetings, if they do not talk about the legislation they are bringing forward. This is good legislation. It is legislation which is long overdue. However, it is being completely undermined by legislation which we are receiving from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde).
It would appear to me that an industrial strategy for Canada must be put in place once and for all, and very quickly. We have been hearing about this industrial strategy for a long time. But how can one department, manpower and immigration, operate in isolation when we do not have an industrial strategy? There is coal development; there is oil development; there are resource developments; there are manufacturing developments. All these developments will take place, not because of the present government, but in spite of the present government. It has to happen. But there must be some co-ordination or we destroy the effects of Bill C-67.
We are setting up manpower and immigration as a reactionary department. In other words, it will react to the alarm bell. The department will react like firemen. There will be a sudden employment crisis or lack of skills in one area, and the department will rush to try to overcome this. Then another one will pop up and it will rush to try and assist in that area. But what it needs is a common industrial strategy so that it can focus all the way through.
I would like to suggest to the minister one way this can happen. If he cannot get co-operative legislation from other parts of the House, what he should be doing is setting up very distinct regional advisory groups, small ones, two, three, or four in each province, which will come together with their recommendations to the minister at least every four months. Since the minister is not getting co-operation now, there is no reason to think that he is going to get it in legislation from other departments. Therefore, he must try and do it himself. The only way he can do this is to try to get forecasts from individuals living in various areas, because they know what is happening and what will be required. That is my major concern, and it is one suggestion I would like to make.
There is a lack of co-ordination in legislation, on the whole. This is a good piece of legislation. I would like to see it passed. I would personally like to see third reading given practically immediately so that the minister and his department can get out there and address the needs which are there. I remember I did suggest that he could amend a few areas, particularly as
they relate to native communities. He should address the energy sector because there is the potential for a real emergency situation coming, because skilled employees are moving south of the border with their rigs. At last count, there were 185. Another 150 rigs will have moved by fall. Skilled workers are going with them, which means we are not going to entice them back. When an energy agreement is reached, they are not coming back because they have signed contracts, some for two years and some for three years.
We will have to retrain in that energy sector again in the western basin, covering the prairie provinces and Alberta. We will have to retrain, so the minister should be targeting in on that. There is a real potential for jobs there; but as I said before, they are being discouraged by the National Energy Program. However, the national energy policy will be changed, I am confident.
Those are the remarks I have. I do hope that I have been able to contribute in a very positive way to this debate. I know the minister is not in the House. I do know, however, that the minister will have his assistant, and so on, reading the remarks which are made when he is not here. I hope that that assistant will take my remarks and put them in front of the minister, because I think they are positive suggestions, and I feel very strongly about them.
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, this bill deals with one of the most important questions this country will have to deal with in the eighties, and that is: How do we ensure that our Canadian population, all Canadians, will be trained to do the many complex jobs that will be opening during the eighties and the nineties as a result of the new technologies of energy developments and so on?
As hon. members know, during the past year I had the pleasure and the honour of chairing the parliamentary Task Force on Employment Opportunities for the '80s which heard hundreds of Canadians on that subject. We heard people from all parts of the country, from Victoria to Newfoundland, and from Windsor to the Northwest Territories. I must say that, in general, the recommendations of those many witnesses have been taken up, to a certain extent, in this bill. This bill does go in the direction that Canadians want to go, but it does not go far enough and it does not cover a wide enough area of reform.
In his remarks last night, the minister said that the goals of this bill, first of all, were to simplify the administration for occupational training in this country by removing much of the paperwork, the red tape and so on. That is an excellent goal and I think would have great support in the country.
The second goal is to make the adult education training programs more flexible. That was a theme we heard over and over again. Very many individuals and groups appearing before our task force complained bitterly about rigidity and inflexibility in the adult education training programs and the manpower retraining programs. That criticism came most often from those parts of the country where unemployment was highest, from the Atlantic region, the Gaspe, the more
July 7, 1981

remote parts of Quebec, northern Ontario and the northern parts of the prairie provinces. They said that many of these programs for retraining and upgrading were probably based on data which came out of the great population areas of the country, such as the Golden Horseshoe around Toronto, the lower mainland of British Columbia and the Greater Montreal area.
1 think that is true to a great extent. Our economic analysts who sit here in Ottawa and carry on their research, for the most part carry out what is called macroeconomic analysis. That macroeconomic analysis deals with the total population figure and national trends, and ends up with solutions which might deal with those national trends; but they do not help very much in many of the slow growth areas of the country. In these slow growth areas of the country the people ask for more flexibility so that the retraining and upgrading programs of the government will suit their needs, be it in northeastern New Brunswick, Cape Breton, the west coast of Newfoundland or northern Manitoba. If the bill achieves that, Mr. Speaker, it will certainly be a step forward.
The minister also said that one of the main objectives of the bill was to deal with the effects of industrial dislocation; that is, where large industries are put out of business or are forced to reduce their manpower needs due to world conditions, such as is the case at present in the automobile industry in southeastern Ontario. When that happens there is a great need to retrain workers who are laid off for new jobs opening up in communities near them or in other parts of the country where great developments are taking place.
I applaud the three goals of the bill, Mr. Speaker. With respect to the specific provisions, the minister said that one of the greatest needs in this country is for more on-the-job training. At the committee hearings we found that less than 20 per cent of Canadian manufacturing industries provided on-the-job training. That is a deplorable figure compared with France, West Germany, Holland and other countries of western Europe where 80 per cent to 85 per cent of manufacturing companies provide on-the-job training. Industries and employers there look upon on-the-job training as an investment in the future, while many Canadian companies look upon it as a cost, not an investment. Consequently, we have a very poor record.
One reason that we have such a poor record is that immigrants were easily available to Canadian companies over the last half century. Whenever trained tool and die makers, welders or machinists were needed, it was easy to take a recruiting team to Europe and pick them up in England, Holland, Germany, Belgium or wherever, rather than spend the money to train native Canadians who, by the way, have remained unemployed because they did not have that chance to be trained. Whether the "carrot" measures, as I will call them, contained in this bill and in present government programs are sufficient to get Canadian companies to provide more training, I do not know. Perhaps we will need "sticks" in
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2 addition to the carrots, and our task force will make some recommendations in that respect.
It was agreed by employers and employees, students and educators that the best type of training they had seen in this country was what we call co-operative education based on the University of Sherbrooke or the University of Waterloo model. This is where the student spends approximately four months in the educational institute and then four months on the job. He alternates back and forth throughout the entire educational process and then when he has obtained his degree or certificate or diploma, he has logged a lot of hours of practical training to go with the academic training. An employer is usually willing to hire him right away. He is not faced with the common answer, "I am sorry, I would like to hire you but you have no experience and I need someone with experience". The co-operative educational model of institutional training combined with on-the-job training will deal with that problem.
There are certain measures in the bill which are laudable and which members of the committee support, although we think the minister could go further. It is, of course, necessary to provide training programs beyond the 52 weeks. Time and again witnesses told our task force that it is impossible to train people for certain skill trades in 52 weeks. The ordinary apprenticeship program in this country is for four years. I think that is too long and in Europe it is two to three years. It is unreasonable to expect to train a man to become skilled in 52 weeks and the measure to extend training beyond 52 weeks is long overdue.
Second, under the present federal legislation a young person had to wait for one year after getting out of high school before he could be financed for an industrial training program. That restriction was harmful to many young people. Many got into trouble or went off and did something else because they had to wait one year, and never returned for skills training. This amendment, which will allow them to go into industrial training even though they have not been out of school for one year, is a good amendment.
Finally, the amendment that will provide for training contracts with other than provincial governments and employers is also good. Provincial governments, through their educational systems and employers, are not the only bodies, that have good training programs. Unions have good training programs and there are non-profit voluntary groups with good training programs. Private schools also have good training programs. We found that some of the best secretarial schools in the country are private schools and some of the best schools for electronic and computer education are private schools. The amendment will allow the minister to conclude training contracts with the unions, with non-profit voluntary groups and with the private schools, associations and groups that provide industrial training or want to provide it.
The other important amendment provides for increased payments for companies that provide the training. Existing industrial training allowances are much too low and give no encouragement to people to come off unemployment insurance or welfare and seek training. If we want a skilled labour force,

July 7, 1981
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
we must finance people through their training period. 1 do not think the measure goes far enough but it is certainly an improvement.
I have said that what is in the bill is laudable, but if we are to deal with this massive problem of skilled-trade shortages in the country and the mismatch in the Canadian economy where high levels of unemployment exist side by side with serious shortages in skilled trades, then much more will have to be done.
When the minister appeared before the committee I asked him whether the bill was the last word and he said that it was not. He said he felt he had to get it through this month or before the summer recess in order to be able to deal with some immediate problems, but that he certainly intended to bring in much wider-ranging amendments to the Adult Occupational Training Act next fall or winter after he had received the report of the task force or the report of the Dodge committee which he tabled in the House today.
I want to mention a few of the other things that have to be dealt with if we are to cope with unemployment and skill shortages in this country. We need a better defined industrial strategy. Representatives for many companies told us that they would be glad to provide more money for on-the-job or industrial training if they knew what the government's approach to their industry was going to be. Spokesmen for the shipbuilding industry told us that if they knew the government's long-range plan for their industry, they would invest much more money in training young people. The same was said by people in the mining industry and other industries. They told us that they had to know the government's industrial strategy before they would invest in very expensive training programs. I urge the government to come forward with a comprehensive industrial strategy program so that we can get on with the training that is needed in this country.
Anyone who is going to build a new factory or establish a new industry cannot expect the skilled labour to appear immediately. It takes from four to seven years to train a skilled workman or skilled professional. It takes at least seven years to train an engineer and for a highly qualified welder, tool and die maker or machinist it takes four years. If we want something to be done for Canadian industry within four years, we should start providing the training today. An industrial strategy is very important.
Another thing that is extremely important and which is not dealt with in the bill is the high rate of functional illiteracy in this country. At the hearings we found out that almost 30 per cent of Canadians are functionally illiterate. That means that they are not even ready or qualified to take the training and upgrading programs provided by the government. Before they would be ready to take those programs, they would have to be trained in basic reading, writing and arithmetic. They have to learn how to read plans, how to communicate, and how to compute before they would be able to take these programs. How can you train a man to be an electrician if he does not have these basic literacy skills? I think it is shocking for a country like Canada to have almost 30 per cent of the population functionally illiterate. People who are functionally illiterate are traditionally the ones who are unemployed. This status unfortunately follows generation after generation. However, we will be dealing with that point in our report.
Even if a lot of money were put into training, if training facilities were expanded and companies were willing to do much more on-the-job training, people will not take that training if the support systems are not there for them. While people are being trained they need at least a living allowance to support themselves and their families. If their homes are at a distance from the training facility, people need the transportation costs to get to the facility. If parents of children are in training, they need a place to leave their children during the day. All of these things cost money. Too many Canadians, and perhaps some government officials, look on those expenditures as transfer payments of one kind or another. But they are not transfer payments; they are really an investment in the future of this country. If we do not get these chronically unemployed and functionally illiterate people trained, the whole industrial output of Canada will be affected.
We heard from many companies that they were unable to expand-this is especially true in the west-and had to turn down orders from abroad because the skilled labour force was not available in the areas where they were set up. If we want to get these people permanently off the welfare and unemployment rolls, we have to be willing to put money into the support systems and into the training necessary for them to become productive Canadians.
There is also the problem of the mobility program, which is not dealt with in the bill but must be dealt with. There is the whole problem of flexible work schedules, part-time work, shared work and flexible retirement.
Finally, if we fill those skilled labour shortages, we have to make sure that the many special groups such as women's groups, native groups and the handicapped have a chance to be trained to do any kind of job in this country, whether it is skilled blue-collar work or professional work. Not only does justice demand it, but economic necessity will require it. If we do not train these women, the native and the handicapped for those jobs, we will not have enough trained people to do what this country demands.
Before closing I want to mention that all of these things could be done better. We need a better forecasting and planning system. We need better federal-provincial co-operation, which I do not think we have now. It is not altogether bad, but it needs great improvement.
I mentioned at the beginning that we are entering the 1980s and 1990s which will be a period of technological change even more rapid than the technological changes we saw in the 1960s and 1970s. If we are to have a more rapidly changing technological age, it means that a man or a woman who is trained at 20 will have to be retrained again at 35, again at 45 and perhaps retrained again at 55.
July 7, 1981

In other words, we will need an educational and training system which will be an ongoing one where people will be able to enter and leave the educational and training system throughout their lifetimes. It will no longer be the style for a child to stay at home from birth to six years of age, attend school from the age of six to the age of 20 and work from the age of 20 to the age of 65, and after that go home and wait to die. Instead we will have a life and a society where we will continually be in and out of the educational and training system, in and out of the workplace, at leisure, at home, taking a sabbatical or whatever. If we are going to meet the industrial and commercial challenges of the 1980s and 1990s and keep Canada a major industrial and commercial nation, we will definitely need much better training, retraining and upgrading systems. This bill goes in the right direction, but we need more.

subtopic: ADULT OCCUPATIONAL TRAINING ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak to Bill C-67, which is a bill to amend the Adult Occupational Training Act. I am pleased because the contents of this bill and the subject of the main act are something which vitally affect all parts of Canda, from Newfoundland to central Canada, on to the Prairies and right through to Vancouver Island. I am speaking of the lack of skilled workers that we have in Canada, and have had for a number of years.
As previous speakers have pointed out, the whole aspect of our society in the 1980s will be changing. We are now into the technological society with more manufacturing, more megaprojects needing more skilled and trained workers. This need will continually increase as we enter the 1990s.
The present system of training skilled workers has been inadequate for the last 10, 15 or 20 years. That is because we have placed too much emphasis and money, not only at the federal and provincial level but also at the municipal level, on the wrong kind of education at the wrong time.
In my opinion, this problem started just after the Second World War. The government in its wisdom allowed every veteran to attend university or other higher learning institutions, and for those who did, their way was paid. That was a very good thing because at that time the country needed people with higher education. In the 1950s, and perhaps even in the 1960s, a university degree was a passport to a job; any kind of a university degree. Admittedly, in the 1940s and the 1950s one could not get a university degree listening to birds or watching flowers or things of that nature. Nevertheless, in order to get employment, people looked to the universities and the universities became pre-employment schools. In a sense they lost a lot of their research capacity perhaps to impart some knowledge and wisdom.
As a result we continued to rely too long on that particular aspect of our training program. This has resulted over the past few years in too many university trained people who we now find are underemployed. We find them doing all sorts of things, even driving taxis. I have nothing against taxi drivers, it is a very honourable profession. I understand that one of the members opposite who recently went to the other place used to
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
drive taxis. Some taxi drivers make a lot of money, sometimes more money than members of this House. I understand also that during the recess some members opposite will be driving taxis to supplement their income. I have nothing against taxi drivers, but I have a lot against trained university people being underemployed.
We used to say that it cost about $8,000 of public purse money, other than tuition fees, to train a person at university. I do not know how much that figure has gone up, but I dare say it has doubled. It probably costs now $12,000 or $16,000 a year.
This year the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) has predicted that there will be 15,000 unemployable university graduates, or a 10 per cent surplus. We cannot afford that kind of misdirection of public funds. The public will not put up with it much longer.
What has been the history of our source of skilled workers? Previous speakers have pointed out how we have relied almost completely on foreign countries to supply our skilled workers. That was a good thing in the past. Earlier in our history we had neither the capacity nor the knowledge to train the kind of skilled people which this country needed.
After the depression and the last war, we were fortunate to have these people come to our land to help develop the frontier, build our cities, our bridges and provide the high standard of living which we have enjoyed and are enjoying. These people from foreign lands have added to the diversification of our society and have enriched it greatly. I am pleased that these skilled workers came to our country.
We are still doing this. For example, 15 per cent of the registered nurses employed in British Columbia are from outside Canada. A recent survey by the Winnipeg Chamber of Commerce showed that some 30 per cent of the skilled workers in that city are from outside Canada. In a report to the committee on employment by the principal of the Pacific Vocational Institute of British Columbia, the largest vocational institute in that province, he quoted figures which are very significant. I would like to read them to the House. He talked about percentages of the Canadian work force. Skilled workers born and trained in Canada amounted to 27 per cent and those born and trained outside Canada amounted to 73 per cent. Almost three-quarters of our skilled workers have been trained outside Canada. What have our federal and provincial governments been doing since World War II?
I wish to place another significant figure on record. Skilled workers in the labour force today who are over 40 years old account for 87 per cent of our work force. Surely that underlines the need for a vast, vital and energetic program to obtain more skilled workers.
The next figure should frighten hon. members most of all. As a percentage of the Canadian work force, presently registered apprentices account for .6 per cent. If that does not indicate the need for drastic action, I do not know what does.
11278

July 7, 1981
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
It is just not good enough in the eighties to rely on foreign countries to supply our skilled worker needs. I say this for two reasons. First, foreign skilled workers are no longer available. It is very difficult for a company in this country to obtain an adequate supply of skilled workers, even by going outside the country and offering very high wages. The economies of Europe, Japan and elsewhere are booming and they need their skilled workers. Second, it is no longer socially acceptable.
The government has estimated that we will need 500,000 immigrant skilled workers in the eighties. When that figure was released, my desk was filled with letters from constituents, mothers and fathers of children who have completed grade 12 and cannot get into a trade school or find employment. These people are up in arms, and I do not blame them. If we cannot train our young people to take the jobs that are available, something is badly lacking. Somebody is to blame. Someone is not doing his job.
One wonders about this tremendous need for skilled workers. Previous speakers have underlined this. Before the national energy policy was announced, it had been estimated that something in the area of $1.5 trillion would be spent on energy and the energy-related field in the eighties. I cannot imagine what $1.5 trillion is other than that it is $1,500 billion. In any event, that is a huge amount to be spent on oil, gas, coal and hydro projects.
The potential is staggering. The hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) gave some of the figures with regard to the spin-off effects. It is in those fields that we need more highly qualified and skilled people.
The government's National Energy Program should not be called the NEP but the NED, "national energy disaster". That policy is so bad it makes one wonder whether it is a deliberate attempt by the Liberals to solve the problem of a shortage of skilled workers. What better way to solve the embarrassing problem of a skilled worker shortage? The NEP is doing that by depressing industry.
Statistics have been quoted about the effects of the NEP. I wish to place on record some statistics with regard to employment. There have been 154 drilling rigs and 84 service rigs leave Canada. By midsummer the total will reach 200. Of the remaining 400, 200 will be idle. According to my calculations,
20,000	jobs will have been lost. That is certainly one way of solving the shortage of skilled workers. However, it will not be acceptable to Canadians, particularly those in the west.
Even without the megaprojects, the employers council in British Columbia, in calculating the needs in that province for the next 20 years by surveying 46 major firms, calculated that 1,338 tradesmen will be required. There are only 577 apprentices in training.
1 wish to quote some of the figures which are relevant and extremely interesting. In the years 1980-81-82, 82 diesel mechanics will be required in British Columbia. Only 16 are presently in training. There will be a requirement for 556 heavy duty mechanics, but only 174 are in training. Fifty-eight electronics technicians will be required and only three are in
training. Surely those figures indicate how short Canada is of skilled workers. At the same time we have an unemployment rate of 7 per cent, 8 per cent or 9 per cent. These people are unable to find jobs.
We have failed badly to solve what should be a basic right in our society. We can fault the unions, the employers, industry and certainly the government. However, often the technical schools have produced the wrong product. For example, they have produced electricians when electricians were not needed. In other words, they were unable to keep up with the requirements of industry. This will probably be even more true in the future when requirements change more radically.
Unions, too, often are at fault for demanding full wages for those people who are under training. Certainly the employer bears a large responsibility for failure to train and to provide training programs for the industry in which they are involved. Most of all, probably governments are at fault, both provincial and federal. They foul up the whole process with bureaucratic red tape.
Let me give one example. In my own constituency we have complaints about the Unemployment Insurance Commission sending people to technical schools to take up the seats they have there in order that they can continue to get their unemployment insurance. They must do this in order to continue to get their benefits. Many times the people who are sent there are not the least interested in training in the jobs they have. They are merely taking up valuable seats which are in short supply in these technical schools, thus preventing people who are interested in getting an education from becoming skilled and getting out into the work force. Certaining the complexity of the problem is immense, and I think I would be the first to admit that.
I have quoted from this study before but it contains some interesting figures. It shows just how wrong governments have been in the past in the kind of approaches they have taken. Companies were asked in 1980: "Has your company an on-the-job training program?", and 71 per cent said they had. The companies were asked: "Has your company ever been in a position of not having sufficient or trained skilled workers?" and 76 per cent said, yes, that was true. They were also asked: "Do you believe your company or your particular industry could benefit from an on-the-job training program?", and this figure is most significant because it confirms what the chairman of the committee who just spoke before me said; 73 per cent said that on-the-job training was the best.
Here is another significant question: "Do you feel the education available from educational institutions could properly train employees in your business?"; 61 per cent answered no. They felt existing educational technical institutions were not capable of training the kind of people they wanted. That says a great deal for the lack of direction and the inability of our existing institutions to move with the times.
I have no objection to Bill C-67. It is a good bill and I think we should pass it. I do not treat it with the same enthusiasm as
July 7, 1981

my seatmate did, the hon. member for Athabasca. I think it is a band-aid approach that is typical of this government. We have a very large problem, but I suppose when your leg is cut off and you are hemorrhaging it is better to have a band-aid than nothing at all.
I feel sorry for the chairman of the Committee on Employment Opportunities for the '80s who spoke ahead of me. Why is the government not paying attention to that committee? Why is the government not waiting until that committee reports? Why is the government not making a comprehensive plan to solve what obviously is one of the worst problems we have to face presently and in the future?
I think those are the kinds of questions that should be answered by the government. It is not good enough for the minister to say: Fine, we will deal with those problems later when the committee reports. He seems to be ignoring the committee and already downgrading what it is going to say by that process of bringing in this bill which deals only with part of the problem. There are obvious areas that have to be looked to and I do not understand why the government has not moved in those areas.
First of all, there should be better reporting and forecasting on both the supply and the demand side. Certainly the federal government is in a position, with its multitude of bureaucrats, its computers and all the other aids it has, to be able to forecast accurately what the supply is and is intended to be, and what the needs are in various parts of the country, so that we can feed this information to the various technical schools and they can gear up and be able to train and provide skilled workers at a time when those skilled workers are required.
What about the target groups that were mentioned earlier, the women and native people? Surely that is where we are going to get most of the additional skilled workers in our labour force. That is where the supply is and certainly the government should be able to move on that. This is nothing new. I have only been in this House for a short time but we have been talking about that since I came here. Does it take 18 months for the government to lay out a simple or a complex plan in order to involve these people, the women and natives who are very anxious to get into the work force and make a positive contribution to this country? I think not, if the government was at all interested, and 1 suggest it is not.
Finally, I think this government should remember that education and training is a provincial jurisdiction. The government would be very unwise to proceed with some of the powers it has under this legislation without the full and complete co-operation of provincial governments. Certainly provincial governments met recently and complained, as previous speakers have said, that there has not been enough consultation and co-operation between the various authorities, and too often the standards the federal government imposes on these training programs are in addition to and often in conflict with those placed by provincial governments.
As the previous speaker said, and I certainly agree with him, there has to be more company-employer involvement. He said 20 per cent of our skilled people are trained by industry as
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
opposed to some 80 per cent in Europe. That is something we can no longer tolerate in this country. Industry will have to solve this problem. If it does not solve it, governments will have to help solve it, either with a carrot or a stick. One of the things I am sure industry fears, being involved in these programs, is the lack of confidentiality. Certainly no company is going to tell their competition what they expect in terms of required employees for the next five or ten years unless they can be assured that this is confidential information.
Those are a few of the things I wanted to speak to in reference to the bill. Again I say I will certainly support it but I express the hope that this government will treat this only as a very interim measure and get on with the problem of finding skilled people to fill the very many opportunities this country will present in the 1980s.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Ursula Appolloni (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: ADULT OCCUPATIONAL TRAINING ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, tomorrow will mark the seventh anniversary of my entry into this House.

subtopic: ADULT OCCUPATIONAL TRAINING ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: ADULT OCCUPATIONAL TRAINING ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
For much of that time I have been looking forward to speaking in this House on this very subject that we are dealing with today, because it is a subject which has very high priority, if not the highest priority in my own riding; that is, adult occupational training.
Last night the minister was good enough to refer to me in his speech. He said I was not too happy with one of the references in the bill, perhaps even more. I do very much welcome this bill; I think it is a step in the right direction. I am even more pleased to note that the minister recognizes it is only one step, because in order to get to a solution to the problem facing Canada today, particularly the problem of unskilled workers, the road is going to be very long indeed, and many steps will have to be taken.
My initial query about this bill can be found even in the title, or more particularly in the definition. The bill now defines an adult as a person whose age is at least one year greater than the regular school-leaving age in the province in which he resides. I shall refer only to the province with which I am most familiar, Ontario, where the school leaving age is 16. Therefore, according to this amending bill, a young adult would have to wait until he is 17 before taking advantage of occupational training. That is my main concern about this legislation.
Why do I stop at the age of 16? Mr. Speaker, a couple of months ago I was fortunate enough, with the tremendous co-operation of the Department of Employment and Immigration and my own local board of education, to initiate a program called the High School Dropout program, which I believe is the first of its kind of Canada. I did this because, like the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), I was personally extremely disturbed about what seems to be an increasing number of functionally illiter-

July 7, 1981
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
ate people begging for jobs. Perhaps not just jobs, but jobs which would pay enough to keep them and their families. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I looked at them and I could not blame the employers for not paying the wages they needed because they did not really merit them. They had nothing to offer the employer, and it was a tragedy.
Looking back over their past histories I realized that more of them in this category had left high school. So we started this high school dropout program in York South-Weston. In essence it is a very simple program. The beauty of it is that it hardly costs anything. What it does involve, though, is very special counselling, and this perhaps is a point which has not been stressed enough in the debate I have heard so far. It is one thing to train people, but before you do that I think the counselling has to be perfect. We can no longer afford to put square pegs in round holes. It has happened too often in the past. Only the counsellor can help find the trainees' real aptitude, so counselling must be absolutely excellent. There are many excellent counsellors in the department, but unfortunately they do not get the recognition they deserve.
The second thing I think we have to be careful of is the attitude of the trainees themselves. I am sure every member of this House has heard complaints from their corporate constituents to the effect: I do not want to hire any more of these people, they do not stay. Perhaps there is a little justification in that complaint.
However, what do you find on the other side of the coin, Mr. Speaker? Well, as an example, we had a youngster in my riding, aged 18, I think, who had been accepted for an on-the-job training program through the Department of Employment and Immigration. His desire was to be a carpenter and his aptitude tests showed he would make an ideal carpenter. He had a tremendous artistic streak in him, too. He would have made an excellent carpenter. So the government helped him with on-the-job training as a carpenter. What happened to him? The first day on the job he was given a finished table leg and told to screw it on the top of a finished table. That was his job on the first day, the second day and the third day. By the end of that week he could not stand it any more and quit.
Now, luckily we were able to help him there, too, because another project in my riding is called the York Home Repair Service, which I started. What do we do? We have three unemployed but skilled workers who teach their skills to six unemployed and unskilled workers, skills such as carpentry, painting, home decorating and minimum repair services. Once they have learned those skills they go out into the community, to senior citizens and low income workers, and they repair their homes free of charge. The home owner has to bear only the cost of materials. The experience these young people gain is terrific. So the youngster who was attaching finished legs to finished tables now makes his own tables and chairs. He can make doors and put them up. We have to give the youngsters this kind of incentive and train them properly.
As to the quality of training, the bill makes reference to this in clause 6(3) where it says there will be consultations between
the commission, the employer and the person, group or association to decide the kind of course to be given. That is a good idea, Mr. Speaker, as far as it goes. However, is that all? Is there going to be a follow up? I am afraid of the abuse which can happen because it has in the past. We have had employers who have accepted incentives from the government to train or hire young people and they have used them as cheap labour without any thought of the consequences for the person involved. I gave you the example already of the youngster and the table legs and tables. This kind of thing has happened too often in the past and I think we have to be very careful to monitor the program so it does not happen in the future.
We should also be careful in the rationalization of this training. There is a Chinese proverb which says if you give a man a fish, you will feed him for one day; if you teach him to fish, you will feed him for a lifetime. That makes an awful lot of sense. However, I think we have to be careful to make sure there is enough water around for him to fish in. Here again there have been pitfalls. I believe on the east coast we trained hairdressers and barbers, too many to look after the population of a given town. This is what I mean when I talk about rationalization of these programs.
I also very much welcome the extended period over which the training program can be held. I have not heard in this debate one particular facet of the extension of this program, perhaps because the members who have spoken so far do not have the same kind of experience I have in Toronto. I have a riding which is blessed with constituents from about 61 different countries. Obviously not all of them are fluent in English or in French. I suppose in Toronto the most important language would be English. However, many of these people who come to Canada have a tremendous aptitude for the very skills we need. Our employment counsellors have verified that the aptitude is there. They perhaps know enough English to get by in a social environment. They can go to the supermarket and converse with their neighbours and what not, but what they are lacking so often, Mr. Speaker, is the jargon of the trade.
It has happened on countless occasions that people who would have made good electricians, mechanics and what have you, were stuck because they did not know the particular words in English for the machinery they were using. People in the medical profession experience a similar situation. They are trained in other countries and come here. Their scientific knowledge is perfect but their language requirements hold them back. When it comes to the definition of occupational training, as in clause 1 of the bill, I hope that the minister agrees to use the broadest possible definition so that people who would otherwise be perfectly willing and able to work in the trade would not be held back because of a lack of knowledge of the jargon of the trade.
Another project was recently started in my riding. I am delighted to say that it is being spearheaded from York South-Weston. It is a project to train women in non-traditional jobs. If I may, I should like to spend a little time on this. It is a
July 7, 1981

subject which has not been discussed sufficiently in the House or perhaps even in the country at large.
When we speak of women in non-traditional jobs, we do so from a very pragmatic point of view. Up to now the government has spent a considerable amount of money training women-and I will stick to my own area because it is the one I know better-for traditional jobs, such as secretarial ones. This is fine. The women are well-trained, they learn, but many of them are single mothers. Unfortunately, at the end of the course the going wage for them will be the minimum wage. There is no mother who can afford to keep herself and her child in Toronto on the minimum wage. Therefore there has been a large attrition rate in this particular field. Women who have been trained in secretarial skills such as typing or whatever have had to abandon their skills at the end of the course when they found that they could not literally afford to work and had to go back to welfare. This is one problem we must face when we speak particularly of single mothers.
What is the solution? In my view there are two. One solution has been referred to very frequently on the west coast in Vancouver. It is a type of phased-in period so that the welfare payments would not be automatically cut off the moment the woman graduated from her training course. It would be phased in until such time as she earned enough to keep herself and her child, particularly for necessities such as medicines and so on which, as we all know, are covered at the moment by welfare. This is one idea. I brought it to the attention of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin). She was most sympathetic and promised to discuss it with her provincial colleagues.
However, I believe in most cases there is a better solution, and that is to train women in non-traditional jobs. Here again we are being very pragmatic because once they graduate from training in non-traditional jobs they will earn very much more than the minimum wage. Once we have said that, let us think of what is really happening.
As I said, the Department of Employment and Immigration agreed to start this pilot project in my riding. Obviously I wanted to help as much as possible. A few months ago I spoke with the area manager who told me that she had a little difficulty with a certain firm in the aerospace industry which, by the way, is doing rather well in Ontario at the moment. She told me that the difficulty was one of attitudes. She did not feel that the company was very co-operative or even very sympathetic to the idea of hiring women who would be trained by the federal government for non-traditional jobs in its plant. This struck her as shortsighted on the part of the company because it is dependent upon the government for its contracts.
However, I telephoned the manager of the company. I asked him if what I had heard was true, that he and his officials had been less than co-operative with the officials of the Department of Employment and Immigration. He blustered, he denied things for a long time, and eventually he said, "Of course, we must not practise inverse discrimination". We will have to tackle this point because it is one of the lamest excuses. It is a new one but it is still lame. Ever since the inception of
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2 this firm, even of the industry itself, discrimination has been practised. Only men were assembling aircraft until the Second World War, when men went out to shoot at others and women had to assemble planes. Is it not funny that no one complained at that time that women were making the planes?
Apart from that, inverse discrimination bothers me because it is so illogical. It is similar to complaining that the pendulum moves only to the right but never to the left and therefore the pendulum is discriminating whichever way it goes. The pendulum will have to swing again to the left in order to get back in the centre where it should be. If this is called inverse discrimination, then I welcome it because it is necessary.
I have heard other hon. members imply that we need the women because we do not have enough men. I do not think women would be too pleased to hear that kind of comment. We need women because they are a wealth of ability and capability. They are a rich resource which we have not tapped enough in the country. I do not want to hear "Yes, we will put women in the assembly line because we do not have enough guys". No, it would not do justice to women. Certainly it would not do justice to the calibre of work we want. It must be first-class all along.
This is the attitudinal problem which we face, sometimes in women themselves. It will take a tremendous amount of public education in order to get over it. But there is another problem when it comes to women in non-traditional jobs. I know some of my colleagues on both sides of the House have already referred to this fact. If we are speaking of women with family responsibilities, no woman I have ever met in my life can take training or do a proper job if she is not first convinced that her child is being properly looked after. Daycare is essential. It is not a hand-out. It is essential that the future generation of Canadians be properly looked after while infants.
I wish the minister were in the House. Perhaps he or his officials could reply to me later in writing. Clause 7 refers to the training allowance. It reads as follows:
The Commission may pay to any adult who is being trained in an occupational training course described in section 5 a training allowance related to the family circumstances-
I would very much hope that these family circumstances would include the serious circumstances of children who need to be looked after while their parents take training.
