speechtext:
Ministers of the Crown are already leaping to the defence of their backbenchers. After paying a compliment I receive hostility.
The parliamentary secretary was very careful not to name de Havilland. I take it from her remarks that it is the firm she was referring to. As she will remember, some of us raised that issue in the House about a year ago on behalf of one of the unions which was petitioning the government with regard to de Havilland's practices. The parliamentary secretary is not saying no to de Havilland, nor is she saying yes. Rather, she is laughing behind her hand and, therefore, I take it that de Havilland is the firm in question. I urge her to raise this issue again with other ministers, such as the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) who has some direct involvement with the employees of that company and who took almost no action at the time this issue was raised.
What happens in that company is a shame. To go even further than the hon. member has, the company appears to have a very direct and deliberate policy of steering women to secretarial jobs and away from jobs on the floor. I have said outside the House, and I will say it inside the House, that it is a most regressive and unfortunate policy.
We raised this issue in the House a year ago and, to my knowledge, nothing has been done about it directly by this government. It is a company which is largely funded by the government. I think the goverment has a major responsibility to demonstrate within companies it owns or funds what it believes should be good practice that all Canadian companies and employers should follow. If it will not set the example then it is in some difficulty when it criticizes others. I say this because I agree with the parliamentary secretary that this issue needs clearing up. I encourage her to continue pressing this issue, if only because we raised it.
I would like to come back to the valuable points made by the parliamentary secretary regarding special counselling by the department of manpower and relate a couple of stories which took place in my riding, since they reflect the difficulties which underlie this act. What seems to happen if you are good at counselling, which is an area quite distinct from training as the hon. member knows, is that you either have to leave the field because you are good at your work-and the only place you can find a substantial promotion is in the private sector-or you are promoted to a position where you are not really able to continue with the direct counselling of people who come to the department for help.
There does not seem to be the other kind of counselling in the department which is critical, which is the counselling of those who will do training assessments. That is a very important hole which needs to be filled. It does not make a lot of sense to have people who want to help the unemployed and those people who need help if they have not been given the proper tools and training in the counselling aspect of the job.
This point came home to me most clearly on Saturday morning when I was in my constituency office and met with a constituent of mine who is currently trying to gain entrance to one of the government's training courses. She knows the problem better than any of us since her career background is in social work, for which she holds a Bachelor of Arts degree. She now has the problem of trying to obtain work in the child care area, after six or seven years of working in that field, only to find that she has been passed over in favour of people with masters' degrees in social work-called MSW's in the trade. Therefore she must pursue a new career, which is unfortunate but which is also a reality.
Thus, she approached the department to see what was available to her and in order to obtain some assistance to determine what she might best be suited for. With her background in the area of counselling you can imagine her shock when she found that the counselling being offered her was inadequate. She related this to me at length, not because she felt the people in the department are poorly motivated or because their intentions are less than honourable, but because she believes that they have not been adequately trained to deal with people in her circumstances.
I now come to the second part of her dilemma. Having decided that she would like to pursue a second career in the area of secretarial sciences which is called word processing, she took the manpower tests for that course and completed them extremely successfully, as one would expect, only to discover two months later that the department was cutting back the program she had applied for. It would appear that, having been accepted into the course, she would have to wait an additional four months to receive the training which the government said it was trying to give her.
It is frustrating to be standing before you, Mr. Speaker, speaking to a bill which has the stated intention of improving training opportunities in Canada while knowing our constituents are having trouble gaining access to existing training programs. While the government says it is taking this course of action to improve the situation, at least in my riding in metropolitan Toronto where unemployment is substantial, it is cutting back on the available retraining programs. It is taking away seats from one of the approved community college courses, at least in the case I have referred to.
Further, it says that once you have chosen the college where you wish to take a course, if the seats are cut back at that college you may not reapply and be reassigned to a different college where seats are available because you have indicated your college of preference. Therefore, you must now wait to receive the training. Where this bill says that what we need is more flexibility, the practice is to create more inflexibility. The
July 7, 1981

good words in the bill would appear not to be met on the ground that the people who are trying their best to deliver programs cannot do so because the strictures placed upon them by departmental rules are inflexible.
1 would like to make this plea, through you, Mr. Speaker. I ask that these representations be taken into consideration by the committee at any time it is dealing with this measure. As a member of the committee I can certainly make a commitment that 1 will be raising these issues. I see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Dawson) is nodding that he might be interested in these areas. That is terrific.
As 1 indicated earlier, on the face of the bill there are a number of matters which are quite exciting and useful. As members will know, for some time one of the problems with retraining programs has been the effect that the payments under retraining have been roughly the equivalent of payments made under unemployment insurance. The bill proposes to increase the allotment for retraining. Let us assume that what seems inevitably to happen with this government will not happen in this case. Let us hope that next year the government will not introduce a bill to increase the unemployment insurance allotment because this year it increased the training allotment. Let us hope that the spread between training and being unemployed, which is presumably to produce an incentive to undergo training-if one believes the government's press releases-will be continued. I believe that is an important point. What is before us is good.
The bill proposes to grant more flexibility to the government in choosing who will be eligible for training and benefits, and in what areas and industries. It reintroduces the usual problem in that at least areas and industries will be designated by the governor in council and not by Parliament or a parliamentary committee. If you look at those areas and industries which qualify, it is amazing the resemblance they bear to ridings held by certain Liberal cabinet ministers. There does seem to be this parallelism which goes on whenever the government brings in this kind of a program, and that is a problem. The idea of the act is to help. We would hope that the help in the act is available across the country where there is a need, and is not simply based on whether one's representative is in the cabinet.

subtopic: ADULT OCCUPATIONAL TRAINING ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ADULT OCCUPATIONAL TRAINING ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Equally, the bill proposes, significantly, to end the limitation which has existed whereby the training programs have only been available for one year. Those who have been involved in this know that sometimes it is necessary to go on longer than a year simply because, as we become an increasingly complex world, the training program takes longer than a year; and that is welcome.
Having described what I think is relatively good, and having indicated that I do believe the bill, while cosmetic in its actual impact, is nevertheless a move in the right direction, there are
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
some matters I want to put on record as being worrisome in the sense that the bill still does not get at them.
Most significantly, as has been previously mentioned, hon. members will know there is a task force meeting now called Employment Opportunities for the '80s. Its members, I gather, to a man and a woman, are opposed to this legislation at this time, and I can understand why. It is because the whole argument about training relates ultimately to the ability of the government to forecast well. There are very real reasons to criticize the government for its forecasting in the past, and yet we are faced with a bill to enter into the training area at a time when the task force on what we ought to be training for has not reported. Therefore, I suspect we will have to see a complete revamping of the government's ability to target for training purposes as a result of that report.
It might have been better if the initiative had waited so that it could take into account all of those things, since the track record in this area is that it takes a long time to get the government to move in training areas. It would, therefore, seem to me that the government is likely to use this initiative as an excuse. What it will say when it does implement the task force recommendations quickly will be, "It is okay, we did a little for you last year with these changes". If that becomes an excuse or is used as a reason to justify not proceeding with what good recommendations do come out of the task force, then we will be back on our feet to say, "We told you at the time that this does not replace a good training program", which we hope will be recommended.
Equally significant is that we continue, as far as I can tell, to have in this bill a provision which allows the government to announce its training initiatives and programs without automatic or necessary resort to consultation with the provinces. The possibility continues to exist that a program will be announced and implemented, and the province consulted after the fact as to whether it was useful. That is a shame. Indicative as it is of this government's attitude toward provincial consultation, which is more evident in other areas which are before this House or may be before this House shortly, it is still, in this case, a shame.
If I can again cite an example of the kind of quandary one gets into when there is not the kind of adequate consultation which should go on, I have a constituent who is desperately attempting to find someone to help him in the particularly innovative area of spot welding. The provincial government has advised the federal government, I gather, that that area should be one of the areas subject to training funds. It is not but should be.
The case could most easily be put this way. This particular constituent applied through manpower for someone to fill this job for eight weeks, as is his right and as is his obligation before he can go anywhere else to find someone. Having done that, having indicated that there was someone from outside the country who could fill the job and do the work which needs to be done in our area, having tried to find a Canadian, the department said, after the fact, "No, we are not going to let you bring anyone in to fill your job need, which may produce

July 7, 1981
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2 more wealth in your area; we would prefer that you train someone." When this man turned around and asked whether there is one of these subsidies to train, the answer was no. The federal government says that that is not an area of need.
That is the kind of problem one runs into when one is dealing with the government and its forecasting ability. When employers take to the government specific areas of job need for which they cannot find people, there seems to be some reluctance to accept what the private sector says is a job need as opposed to what the statistics say is a job need.
I might point out an example found in Toronto. I use this example gently because I do not want to offend any of the people in the florist business. However, one of the programs which is currently regarded by the department as being in demand, and therefore subsidizable, is one which shows up on the form as "floral design". I should say that when I first saw it on the list it reminded me of those of us who went through college in the last 15 or 20 years in the country, which is what the government told us we ought to do in order to get a job. Even if we did so by taking courses in basket weaving or other things, that was okay. A degree was going to get us a job. That was the government's forecast 15 years ago, and it is now showing up as being disastrous. I am therefore suspicious whenever I see a government list of occupations there will be a demand for, so I called. No one can tell me where that demand is; no one can yet tell me how many people are needed in it; and no one so far has been able to tell me why it is on the list. That is a little worrisome when one is being asked to support this kind of program.
Therefore, I believe that while we may not have the perfect system when we rely on provincial forecasting, at least it is a component of the forecasting system which is somewhat closer to the ground, in real need, than Ottawa. I hope we will see a reliance on provincial forecasting rather than the apparent ability in this bill to get around it.
If I might put on the record some of the problems which exist in that area, probably a report which would be of interest to anyone concerned with this subject is an Economic Council report called the Betcherman report, which deals with these figures and lists some of the existing situations where the government has said it knows what we need to spend money for and what the realities are. Perhaps some hon. members might be interested in some of these numbers.
Effectively, what the report would seem to say is that in the past funds have been spent in a relatively haphazard manner and not targeted to specific skills which are needed in certain locations, which is what should be done. For instance, the most critical shortages are in product fabricating and repair, machining and science engineering, but training is seldom targeted to meet those needs.
These are some examples. Product fabricating and repair accounts for 22.3 per cent of the shortages in Canada, but only 19.4 per cent of training programs, and only 27 per cent of those programs are government funded, according to that report. Equally, according to the report, machining personnel, who account for approximately 32 per cent of the government
assistance today, account for 13.4 per cent of the shortage in Canada, and only 8.8 per cent of the training programs. Science and engineering workers, the third highest need group, account for 12.2 per cent of the shortage and yet only 5.9 per cent of the training programs, and less than 17 per cent of the total government aid. In other words, as the Betcherman report pointed out, groups for which we actually have a shortage are not adequately perceived by the government, and we do not get a proper response to the facts of the real world.
Sometimes-and this is a matter that the bill does not address-we find we are training in the wrong skills, or we are not even training enough in the skills which are needed. That, unfortunately, often winds up with lowering the employment standards for workers already in the force, and therefore often puts people in a position whereby they are competing for jobs which are already filled as opposed to filling jobs which are vacant in industries which need help; and a whole series of problems can arise from that.
Finally, let me return to the view which I think many of the hon. members on this side of the House will be presenting, which is a view which most of us hold. I believe we will be supporting this bill, from everything that I can see, not because it is a major initiative in the area, and not because it solves the training problems of the adult unemployed in Canada, but because it goes a little way toward producing some more flexibility if the department chooses to implement it. This is critical-if the department chooses to implement it. It would give some more opportunity and incentive to those who are unemployed to choose to take training work.
However, we hope-and this will be the plea, I believe, of those of us who have been in this area for some time-that the government will take seriously its stated goals toward employment development and that it will take seriously the recommendations when they come from the Employment Opportunities Task Force. As I said earlier, I hope that we will not, as I fear, receive any claims from the other side, here or in public terms, that the government has provided, through this bill, a major and sufficient initiative in the area of adult training. Because it clearly is not that. It is an important but small matter. I hope it is understood by hon. members opposite and by the minister that it is in that vein that those of us who rise to support the bill do so, in order to remind him that we expect better from the government. We will continue to press for that.

subtopic: ADULT OCCUPATIONAL TRAINING ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak in this debate on the amendments to the Adult Occupational Training Act. As a member of the task force on Employment Opportunities for the '80s, I had a unique opportunity to travel across the country and listen to the views and concerns of many Canadians with respect to the manpower training programs, the employment programs in the Canada employment centres that have been established by the government to assist unskilled and unemployed individuals to find better jobs and get better training.
July 7, 1981

As a result of the hearings, I have become aware of the importance of these amendments to our training policies. As the task force nears the end of its mandate, all its members have arrived at a deep interest in any changes in the policies that provide Canada with the skilled workers necessary for the continuation of our economic advancement into the next decade.
The task force has heard from hundreds of concerned groups of employers, workers and educators over the last year. Most have called for changes in the way which the federal government funds and oversees training programs now in existence in Canada. This experience has made me aware of the pressing need for fundamental revisions in our educational and training programs.
These experiences have made members of the task force aware that the present Adult Occupational Training Act is inadequate. There has to be more flexibility in the program to allow employers and employees to benefit from training programs with a minimum of red tape and administrative hassle. This bill now before the House represents a good beginning in the process of reform.
With the determined and co-operative efforts of all parties in this House and our provincial counterparts, we will be able to provide all Canadians with a secure and prosperous future. We all know that the supply of skilled workers is fundamental to our national economy. No one can argue against that point. We are all aware that the apprenticeship and training programs now in existence do not adequately meet our present demands, let alone those of the future.
In order for the economy to expand, we have to stress the importance of new technologies. These advancements will require skilled workers to see them carried out. We must have skilled workers in order to become more competitive in the marketplace; we must manufacture better products and be able to supply, to sell, and create new markets which will expand our economy and make more job opportunities. We have to be able to provide the manpower necessary for an adaptable economy, and therefore we have to have a labour pool which has the basic skills for any job as well as the skill levels to be readily adaptable to new employment requirements and opportunities. We cannot continue to rely on temporary solutions and catch-up measures in our employment policies and we certainly cannot continue to rely on offshore workers. Therefore, we must have a comprehensive skills training act which will eliminate the double-edged problems of high unemployment and skilled labour shortages.
There has to be a strong national manpower policy which will begin to eliminate regional manpower imbalances. This policy has to have clearly defined goals, aimed at ending shortages in some fields and surpluses in others. What is needed is a flexible set of solutions. The federal government has to lead the way.
1 concede, Mr. Speaker, that many of the problems have arisen as the result of poor planning on the part of the government and its inflexibility in the past. Problems have also arisen because of the approach of provincial government edu-
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
cational institutions to higher education and their emphasis on post-secondary education. Wherever the fault lies, it is clearly indicated that the federal government must take the lead.
The bill under consideration today is but one step in this direction, and I believe it is a step in the right direction. The basic aim of Bill C-67 is to provide the federal government with the flexibility necessary to increase access to, and availability of, training programs. Any new program has to account for the fact that not all skilled trades can be learned in 52 weeks. Therefore, Bill C-67 provides for increased allowances for courses which last over one year. Not all training programs will last this long, as some skilled trades can be learned in the period now allowed by old regulations. This new extended length provision will allow Canadian workers to train for skills which demand more comprehensive training programs and training time.
Another welcome provision which has been included in Bill C-67 is the one where, under certain conditions, funding can be made available for training programs not available in Canada. This will allow a number of Canadian workers to train outside the country and then return home with the knowledge to implement these learned skills in national production. Our training policies and programs will then have the ability to reproduce newer technologies in Canada.
It is very important in the field of resource development that as new and innovative approaches are taken in other countries, Canadian industry, particularly in the forestry and mining sectors, is able to send abroad some of their better workers to be trained in new technologies for processing and timbering. The companies would then have better trained workers and this would raise productivity levels. This change, to allow employees to go outside the country for upgrading and higher skills does not question the capabilities of our Canadian schools; rather, it broadens our capabilities, which are presently footed on a strong base, to meet the needs of the future.
One of the major criticisms of the training programs that we heard as we travelled across the country concerned our young people having to wait a full year after leaving school before they qualify for training programs. Bill C-67 includes provisions whereby funding schemes will become more responsive to the needs of Canadian industries. With this provision, the employment commission could waive this condition and allow a number of young people to enter the training system without a long wait. As a result, skilled workers will enter the job market earlier and this will provide the incentive for more pre-employment training in our schools.
Another example of this bill's flexibility is the fact that it allows the employment commission to channel funding to areas where there is a demonstrated skill shortage. This is the kind of flexibility that a great number of submissions to the task force recommended. Not all of the new amendments deal with young people. In order to eliminate the possibility of older workers losing their jobs because of plant shutdowns and redundancy, Bill C-67 allows the commission to fund training programs to update their skills. This will eliminate one of the major problems the economy faces with respect to loss of

July 7, 1981
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2 skilled workers or not having them available for better training or being unable to train our young people.
The most important aspects of Bill C-67 are the provisions which will eliminate some of the red tape which until now has stopped a large number of firms from beginning training programs. A recent survey showed that only 20 per cent of all firms have training of any sort. In that same survey it was reported that only 15 per cent of all employees in Canada have received any training at all. This tragic situation has to be eliminated.
This bill will eliminate to some extent the red tape which caused some smaller firms to create an administrative job just to fill out the forms required to receive grants. I believe the bill will reduce this bureaucratic red tape and create incentives for smaller companies to apply for grants under the act so that they may provide more training opportunities for their workers and thus supply more skilled workers.
By providing for flat-rate payments to industries and fixed-rate payments to the provinces, most of the guess work has been taken out of the system. All the small employer has to do is ensure that the programs meet the criteria set out in the regulations and apply for reimbursement. This is especially important to the smaller firms which cannot afford the administrative costs required under the old regulations.
Besides allowing for less administrative work for companies when applying for funds, the act allows the commission to enter into contracts with persons other than employers for the creation of training programs.
As we travelled across the country, we heard that some private businessmen are better able to train individuals than the local institutions or the local major employer. I think the new provisions will give some skilled people who want to go into the private marketplace the opportunity to sign contracts at Canada employment centres to train individuals where and when they are needed. It will not always be necessary to rely on the local employer to do so. This will enable Canadian workers to train for new jobs in areas where there is a demonstrated shortage.
Therefore, these amendments provide the federal government with the flexibility to meet the changing employment market. Companies will have greater incentive to begin training programs, employees will see the benefits of learning new skills, and our young people will begin to have a clearer picture of their future in the Canadian job market.
In conclusion, I believe these amendments are a good start. They open the door to a serious re-evaluation of our total training programs. I know that some members opposite have some concern that this bill should be delayed until the employment task force has an opportunity to present its report and to have its recommendations embodied in the amendments to Bill C-67. Indeed, the hon. member for Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley), who spoke before me, presented that very argument; he did not want to see the government use Bill C-67 as the excuse to put an end to its proposed changes to the Adult
Occupational Training Act. For the benefit of the hon. member for Don Valley West, I shall quote from the speech made by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) last night. As reported at page 11239 of Hansard, we read:
Some hon. members have asked me for the assurance that passage of this legislation will not close the door to further changes in training legislation after the studies have been considered. I am pleased to offer those assurances. As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, the amendments introduced in debate on second reading are simply the prelude to a much wider range of changes that must take place.
I intend to take the minister at his word. I hope that this bill will receive third and final reading. But I want to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the passage of Bill C-67 will not, and should not, be considered the end of the government's initiatives in manpower training policies. Other members of the Task Force on Employment Opportunities for the '80s and myself will continue to push for changes once our report is released some time this summer. That report will include a wide range of recommendations. Some of those recommendations will be simple administrative changes that will be necessary and will have to be implemented by the department. Other changes will be more drastic, and perhaps even of an alarming nature. I think I can speak for many members of the task force in saying that we intend to see that those recommendations are listened to and carried out by the government.
Therefore, I welcome these amendments. But I wish to remind this House that these amendments can only be considered as a preliminary step towards a total re-examination, and re-evaluation of programs as well as a complete redirection of Canada Manpower programs and human resource planning in this country.

subtopic: ADULT OCCUPATIONAL TRAINING ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in this debate on Bill C-67, to amend the Adult Occupational Training Act, which proposes a number of amendments to this act that are very much needed and have been a long time in coming.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) in his opening remarks on this bill yesterday said, as reported on page 11239 of Hansard'.
The bill we are studying today has three basic goals. The first is to simplify the administration of the Adult Occupational Training Act and to eliminate much of the unnecessary paper work that small businessmen in particular must face in developing industrial training on the shop floor.
That particular amendment is welcomed by me and I am quite sure it will be advantageous to small businessmen in the administration of this act. The minister went on to say:
Second, we want to make the act more flexible so that it will respond to the variety of needs in the training area.
As I read those words of the minister, I see as usual he is full of hope that these measures will go a long way to solve not only our skills problems but also our unemployment crisis. I was rather interested to hear the previous speaker say, once again on behalf of the government, that this program is not a program to end all programs in terms of job creation, but is simply just the beginning in a long process.
I have been here for some 18 months and I followed the debate in this House rather closely prior to coming here. It seems to me the government is always making statements like that but it never does anything in a concrete way about any job-creation programs, at least in the long term.
While the minister was on his feet yesterday, in recognizing the changes in our society being brought about by technological change, he said:
While service work-work in the areas of public administration, clerical, management, health services, education and others-was the major stimulus for growth in the last two decades, it will increasingly decline as a supplier of jobs in Canada.
In the next paragraph the minister said:
We must promote the integration of women, native people and disadvantaged workers in a larger field of employment. We must train more workers in skilled trades and occupations. We must help the workers already on the labour market to learn new skills without undue difficulties.
While amendments to this act have been a long time coming and are welcome, I think the minister is dreaming if he believes that these amendments will solve both our unemployment problem and the lack of skills training in our work force.
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
Approximately 7.1 per cent of our population, or over one million Canadians, are unemployed. Close to half a million young people under the age of 24 are without work, and it is estimated that 50 per cent of those have less than a grade 10 education.
In the over-all scheme of things, the most that can be said of this bill is that it will improve the present inadequate legislation, but without additional policies it is simply a continuation of the government's cosmetic approach to these deep-rooted problems.
I find it interesting that the minister can wax so eloquently about the virtues of these amendments in terms of doing something concrete about the serious lack of skills training, when he knows, as do the unemployed, that there are simply very few jobs available in the marketplace. I would have been much more impressed had the minister come forward and told us that he recognized the very real problems we have and that he would present to the House an over-all strategy to solve them. But the minister has not done that. All he has done is forward some improvements to an inadequate piece of legislation which, even though welcome, do very little to treat the whole problem.
Surely the time has come for the government to recognize that we cannot seriously discuss the present lack of occupational skills training without talking about a full employment strategy. I suggest, as some members on the government side have suggested, that you cannot at this time in our history continue to ignore the needs for integrated strategies to treat the serious problems we face as a country and as a nation. In my view, you cannot talk in a serious way about job training without talking about industrial strategy. You cannot talk about an industrial strategy without talking about an economic strategy and a social policy strategy. I say that for a few reasons.
Earlier in my remarks I spoke about the general unemployment problem. However, the hidden unemployment figure is closer to 1.25 million. We do not include in this group of Canadians out of work another element in our society. I am referring to people who are considered to be disabled or handicapped in our society. They are not regularly included in the unemployment figures, neither the seasonally adjusted nor the actual figures.
I was a member of the Special Committee on the Disabled and Handicapped which recently tabled its report in the House. The report itself points out that while we have something like 2 million Canadians who are considered to be disabled or handicapped, or 10 per cent of the population, out of that group there are 700,000 disabled Canadians who are considered to be employable. In that particular segment of the population there is an unemployment rate estimated to run between 70 per cent and 80 per cent. The committee viewed this so seriously that, out of the 130 recommendations it made in that report, 19 centred on the unemployment problem.

July 7, 1981
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
While there are numerous problems faced by disabled Canadians that able-bodied Canadians are faced with, such as housing, education, transportation, recreation, communications and unemployment, none of these problems can be separated from the others. One is synonymous with another. If you want to provide people who are disabled and presently in institutions with adequate accommodation, transportation and access to educational facilities, you have to provide them with the means to do that. That is why the committee placed such emphasis on employment opportunities. Even with the special employment program which the minister brought forward earlier this year that was supposedly directed toward disabled Canadians, it is generally recognized within the disabled community that that program will do very little, if anything, to provide those who are disabled with jobs, particularly those who are physically handicapped.
The minister talks about the amendments to this act doing something in a very real way to provide employment opportunities or skills training opportunities to disabled and handicapped Canadians. He is kidding the troops, he is kidding himself, but he certainly is not kidding the disabled and the handicapped, and he is not kidding me. The amendments in this bill will not do anything for those who are disabled and require an upgrading in skills training. For the minister to make those kinds of statements is, as I said earlier, kidding the troops.

speechtext:
As my friend from for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) says, he is good at that, but he has not been so good recently, especially among women's groups, which is another area I want to talk about.
While the minister seems to recognize that society is changing very rapidly in terms of skills as applied to traditional jobs, there is an area that will change even more rapidly than it has up to this point. This is the area of clerical work, which will change rapidly as a result of electronic applications. For example, the impact of the microchip on the industrial work environment will have major repercussions on the structure of the work force as we presently know it. There is justified concern that those most likely to bear the brunt of the inevitable change will be those working in information processing occupations, and particularly in service industries. A West German study predicted that 40 per cent of office work could be eliminated within ten years. A French report forecast that 30 per cent of bank employees could be redundant within the same period. In Britain, a study predicted 25 per cent unemployment by 1990.
How fast the changes impact are a source of disagreement, but most experts agree that certain jobs will become redundant as new, relatively inexpensive machines with computing functions, such as word processors, do the work faster and more efficiently than the people now holding the jobs.
There is no consensus on whether more jobs will be created or lost, but women will probably face the brunt of it more quickly. Women are concentrated in clerical, sales and service jobs involving the straight handling of information, and it is these jobs that will be transformed. About 80 per cent of Canadian working women are in the service-producing sector of the economy. One and a half million women-34 per cent of working women-are employed in clerical jobs alone. In federal government secretarial work, the percentages go as high as 90 per cent. Therefore, jobs traditionally held by women are expected to suffer disproportionately from the microelectronics revolution.
The problem is predicted to be not so much displacement as much as a tendency not to hire the additional person. Attrition will also play a part. For example, with the introduction of the electronic switchboard, the number of operators on toll boards in Toronto dropped to 664 in October, 1978, from 1,048 in September, 1977. I understand that that work force has been reduced even more dramatically from the 1977 figure. But there were no lay-offs as such, partly because the turnover rate of operators is extremely high.
The changes are almost certain to create a skills gap. Some existing jobs will be downgraded as machines take over computing and sorting functions. When word processors were introduced in a large Calgary firm, the secretaries were freed of 50 per cent of their usual workload. At the same time, jobs created by the new industry will require more skill and aptitude.
Extensive retraining may be necessary for women if they are to get their fair share of the new employment. Without retraining, women may well end up in the lower paying jobs. For example, women tend to fill the minimum wage production line jobs in the high technology firms in the Ottawa area. Women are underrepresented as computer progammers, analysts, accountants and engineers, among other occupations where computers are expanding employment opportunities.
Observations noted in "Women and the Chip" included the fact that, at the clerical occupation level, labour requirements are seemingly being reduced in the following ways. First, there has been a reduction in the clerical steps involved in handling, processing, storing and distributing information. Second, there has been an erosion of the labour component of clerical functions. Third, there is a telescoping of the supervisory and low level administrative requirements.
At the specialist and professional occupation levels, labour requirements are seemingly being intensified in the following ways. First, automation of the clerical and administrative detail content of the job; and second, escalation of the job's scope and potential with computer aids, such as computer modelling and data processing.
Several dangers were identified in "Women and the Chip". Among them were the following. If women continue to be concentrated in clerical positions and if these continue to be usurped by automation, by 1990, if present trends continue, they could contribute substantially to the unemployment rate. The skills difference between clerical and technical-profession-
July 7, 1981

al occupations could widen to the point of certain discontinuity between the two levels if present trends continue. If women are not able to bridge the occupational gap, industry could face a severe skills shortage in the specialist-professional occupations.
There is a need for immediate policy action on a number of fronts, such as training programs and educational leave opportunities, to enable women to acquire the necessary understanding of computer technology and the skills to make computers enhance their work and employment opportunities, instead of the reverse.
We need occupational bridging and other mobility programs, preferably giving legal clout in affirmative action agreements, which are necessary to ensure that women gain access to occupations being enhanced by computer technology. There is a need for health and safety concerns, such as stress, eye strain, back problems and the possibility of radiation exposure.
The federal government has been very slow to respond appropriately to the coming crisis. Most women taking manpower training courses continue to be slotted into secretarial and clerical classes, the very occupations which are going to be hit hardest by technological change. Entrance rates by women into non-traditional courses have been very slow and sparse, and part of the problem is the stereotyped bias of manpower counsellors who need some counsciousness-raising courses. The present training allowances, in my view, are a joke. As of August, 1979, the dependant care allowance of $10 per week per dependant was limited to a maximum of $40 per week.
In my view, manpower training courses must expand their shopping list to reflect predicted job vacancies and must offer incentives so women represent at least half the enrolment in these courses. Ancillary amenities, such as the training allowance, must more realistically reflect real cost so they do not serve as a deterrent to women trying to upgrade their job skills.
The federal public service should offer retraining to its employees, free of charge and during working hours. Women who have to pay for a class and daycare, plus add a third job to the two they already hold in the paid labour force and in household tasks, are unlikely to pursue more responsibility.
Affirmative action must be expanded throughout the federal public service and should be enforced through contract compliance with the private sector. The federal government does $11 billion worth of business with private firms. It should use this clout to ensure the removal of barriers to career development for women and to systematically ensure better access to employment possibilities.
Finally, the number of women's Outreach projects should be substantially increased, since they focus on the particular needs of women. Only by careful planning can the impact of microtechnology on women in the work force be cushioned. Retraining and occupational bridging can mitigate the coming skills gap if programs are started today. The federal government must start concrete action now to ensure that the wave of
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
new technology does not break on the backs of women in the labour force.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a few comments on Bill C-67. I listened with interest to other speakers and I will not be able to speak with the eloquence of members who were on the task force. I listened to the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand), the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Lonsdale), the hon. member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) and the hon. member for Beaches (Mr. Young) who were on the committee. They made some very important comments regarding this legislation.
I also think it is important that we deal with something that in our brief period of government we wanted to encourage and use more than had been used in the past. That was a system of encouraging members to be part of a task force. Members of Parliament could use their talents to study important issues in this nation, to build upon those studies recommendations which would be presented to Parliament, not just to the minister for his use or non-use, but to Parliament, so that members of Parliament would have these words of wisdom through a study done by members of Parliament elected by the people of this nation to assist in their government.
What we see happening with this bill is that it is before us before the parliamentary task force has reported to Parliament. This, in my opinion, does not make a lot of sense. If we place some value in the report that is coming forward, surely this type of legislation should wait for the advice of that task force. Then the measure could be altered in those areas where recommendations are made.
We started the procedure. We had four task forces set up. They were passed by Parliament, given a chairman and members to work on a number of topics, including volunteers, the disabled. We anticipated something on nuclear policy. We had task forces on branch line abandonment and emergency grain movement legislation. Two of those committees were able to report and those reports had a significant impact on what government did in those areas. This gave us as members of Parliament some encouragement that we had some value in this place. When we participate on standing committees we often find, more often than not, that the minister and the government are not prepared to accept any amendments from members of Parliament from other parties, or even their own party. They decide that the bureaucrats who advise the minister, and the minister who has put his stamp of approval on a bill, know all and there shall be no changes. That is why we get so frustrated as we participate in the standing committees and witness our inability to improve legislation; and it is why we have to move many amendments in this House at the report stage. We do not feel we have been given adequate hearing at the committee, or adequate hearing in the country through the only means many of us have, and that is the news media.
I heard the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) stating on "Question Period", I believe, a television show on Sunday, that he was concerned about Bill C-57 which came before the House with over 100 amendments. I say we are all

July 7, 1981
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2 concerned about that, but this concern results from a feeling, on the part of opposition members in particular, that we are not given an adequate hearing in committee, that the government is too inflexible and, therefore, we have to bring these amendments to the floor of the House, putting them before this chamber so we may get a little assistance from the people of this nation as a whole. That is why the system of task forces is so important to this House of Commons.
As I read the excellent reports on the disabled and handicapped, on North-South relations, the proposed trading corporation and hopefully soon in this area-I understand the task force will report some time this summer-I note adequate studies have been done with very important recommendations being made. These are recommendations the government should be encouraged to accept, maybe not in whole but in good part. This would serve the country well.
I remember serving on a task force on emergency grain transportation and the government accepted the majority of the recommendations. That was the only light we have seen in western Canada regarding grain transportation for a good number of years. I would like to encourage the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to begin to deal with that very quickly as we see a very good crop being produced on the prairies, but no initiative being taken by the government to obtain hopper cars and other rail facilities to move that crop.
That is an example, and we had the example of the branch line abandonment study, which was accepted by this government, put into place and which served the farmers of western Canada very well. We now come to this task force which will be reporting this summer, but we have before us a bill to deal with the very subject that committee is studying and are without its advice. I really think that is not advisable and actually is flying in the faces of members of Parliament who are serving on that task force.
The previous speaker spoke of the need of the governments of this nation to deal with the decades of the 1980s and 1990s. We are moving rapidly into the era of the computer and the robot, which have the capacity to displace people from the work force. It has been said in a number of studies I read recently that many people in the next two decades will have to change their occupation, some as many as ten times. A wage earner with one skill becomes a little apprehensive of this kind of study because he is concerned that maybe he will not have the kind of skills necessary if his job becomes redundant or is lost to new technology or competition. That is why this bill or one like it is important, because we have to encourage our people to train and retrain.
It is also important that the provincial and federal government co-operate in providing the kind of education which will prepare our young people for retraining and for accepting new challenges beyond what they can now envision. Movie theatres are doing an excellent job of showing what is ahead of us. Some of it is very speculative, but I think it shows that the computer and space technologies, which have provided a tremendous number of innovations to the industrialized world, really can influence the work habits and jobs available to our citizens.
Now, I look at my province of Alberta which has just announced that a $100 million training centre will be built. The two centres we have, one in Calgary and one in Edmonton, which teach skills to young and old alike in the technical trades, are inadequate because of the demand in western Canada for skilled labour. We also have a community college which is doing an excellent job. So this announcement is an excellent initiative, but obviously even by the time it comes on stream it will probably be inadequate to meet the demand for the kind of projects envisioned in western Canada. In the past, when megaprojects such as the Syncrude project have been proposed, labour had to be imported from across the country to meet the need. Well, this time, if we approve two additional projects larger than Syncrude, will we be able to supply the skilled labour necessary and at the same time supply the petrochemical plants and the needs of the rest of the nation? I speak only of the needs of industry in Alberta because I am familiar with it. I refer to the pipelines, the new types of welding and the new types of skills needed for deep drilling which are much different than in the past.
What I am attempting to say is that not only does our province need to provide this kind of assistance, perhaps other provinces do as well, and the federal government must co-ordinate and assist in areas such as secondary education and on the job training. Members have stated that in the nations of Europe which have had more experience in this area about 80 per cent of job training is done by the companies. They consider it an investment in the future. Here in Canada only 25 per cent of our skilled trades people are trained here. I suppose in the past we have been dependent a good deal on immigration. We have stated a need; if we could not fill it here, we went abroad and tried to attract people. Often this was done to the dismay of these countries because many of them could not afford to lose these skilled people.
So far as training of our own people is concerned, there are two groups we have really overlooked. Those two groups are native people and women. I think women could be very much affected by new technology. Whether we like it or not, many women in this nation are employed in secretarial and clerical jobs which in the future may largely disappear.
Now, these two groups can benefit from retraining and we must prepare ourselves for that. When I looked at this bill in preparation for speaking on it, I was not very encouraged. When I look at my constituency in Alberta, and when I look at a government bringing in reasonably good legislation, 1 see the same government bringing forward legislation which, at the same time, is driving skilled people out of my constituency and my province. My constituency happens to produce a good amount of Canada's conventional oil. When things were going well a couple of years ago, many Canadian entrepreneurs, people who had learned their skilled trades from the large oil companies-which seem to have such a dismal image at the present time, companies such as Imperial Oil, Shell Canada,
July 7, 1981

Gulf Canada and so forth-decided it was time to grab hold of this industry. They went out and expanded industrial parks, built their own facilities and began to challenge these companies or to work with them in a farm-out type of operation. In fact, for many of them their life's blood was a farm-out to a large oil company so the land they bought for the province could be drilled. Then along came the NEP and the government destroyed 40 per cent of the budget of these companies and literally killed many of those struggling new entrepreneurs in my riding who were attempting to make their way in this industry.
As of June 17 we have lost 150 rigs to the United States with a resulting 20,000 unemployed. We have 221 rigs working in Canada and 237 which are not. I was talking to a friend of mine on the weekend who is involved in the trucking industry. He said that basically in the last two months he has hardly moved anything at all. His whole business was trucking rigs into the northern part of the province. What I am saying, Mr. Speaker, is that here we have a bill to retrain individuals, yet we are sending our skilled people to the United States, those who were learning their trades and teaching others. I am sure the United States are very pleased. They realize how important it is to have energy self-sufficiency and not be at the whim of some foreign government. They are very encouraged by our sending people down there.
This bill says that areas and industries have also been designated by the governor in council for increased assistance of up to 70 per cent of income for individuals entering apprenticeship. They listed the automotive assembly industry in Windsor, primary metals in Sydney and the shipbuilding industry. We may well need that in our province, if we ever get the two governments together, to retrain individuals in the oil industry because we are losing them to the United States.
I should like to refer to the numbers of people who are being lost in my own constituency where a study of 41 companies was undertaken. They conducted a poll to which 41 companies responded. The summary showed that total sales for 1980 dropped from $225 million to $218 million. This was in 1980 when the budget was first announced. Approximately $38 million was lost in that little area. It is forecast that in 1981 there will be a drop from $277 million to $174 million worth of work. This is a loss of $102 million in a few companies in my riding. This can be projected because in that area there are some 300 or 400 companies involved in this business. Also the study indicated a loss of 255 jobs because people had moved with the rigs to the United States, as well as a loss of 173 jobs in branch and field operations.
If this is projected to other areas of the province such as Drayton Valley, Brooks, Red Deer and so forth, it is a phenomenal amount of lost expertise, skilled labour and capital, all of which we need desperately in the country. They have been lost to other countries because of our policy-because of the Liberal policy.

speechtext:
It is important that the citizens of the nation know whose policy it is.
I should like to speak for a few moments about a specific group of people. When the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) brings forward bills, I feel this group is left out. Again they are left out of Bill C-67, which is so important to that group of people. They, above any other group in the nation, learn and benefit more from on-the-job training, much more so than from secondary and technical schools. I suppose the reason for this is that the record of getting these people through our educational facilities has been very poor. This bill will not benefit this group of people.
I do not know how many times I have quoted the native unemployment statistics in the House. I wonder whether the government listens. The government tabled its own report last year, but I think it is important to give the statistics repeatedly so that members will be aware of the problem. The unemployment rate of natives in the summer is as high as 50 per cent and rises to as much as 90 per cent in the winter. There is a great dependence upon social assistance because of this.
1 should like to refer to the study on Indian conditions which indicates that in 1970 federal government social assistance to native people amounted to $34 million. In the 1978-79 fiscal year, it rose to $104 million. Turning to the area of child care, there is the problem of broken families and families unable to keep their children because of unemployment. In that event the provincial foster care people come in and remove the children. To a large extent they are placed in non-native homes.
I believe the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) is addressing this problem. It is very important because once these children are removed from their cultural background-and historically they have no choice because they are enclosed in reserves-they become additions to the statistics as they grow older. The costs for child care have doubled from approximately $11 million to $24 million. The cost of trying to cure alcoholism, which is a very desperate problem among native people, rose from $167,000 in 1970 to $5.5 million in 1978. Even today that sum is inadequate, and it has probably risen by another couple of million in the last two years. The expenditures for other social services have risen from $1 million to $10 million, that is, adult care and welfare aid. The cost of medical services has risen from $36 million to $94 million.
The problem is that most of the Indian social assistance or medical assistance is not directed toward prevention; it is directed toward dealing with the after effects of the problem. Many of the things that we as citizens of the nation take for granted are not available to most native people. The expenditure on preventive measures such as sports and recreation rose from $97,000 in 1970 to only $2 million in 1978. This is something which should have risen faster; in fact it has not risen at the same rate as inflation.

Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
The report also indicated that the cost of native people living off federal government social welfare has increased from $84 million in 1970 to $242 million today. This means that the economic development, job training and preventive service programs in many areas are failures. They are not working. They are not providing the type of assistance the government should provide to deal with these problems. It is only one statistic with which we must deal.
I should like to turn to the number of jobs which need to be created. The only way to have any success would be through training, not retraining because most native people do not have or have not been able to acquire any skills because of the situation in which they live. The government creates approximately 3,000 jobs a year for status Indians, but we need an additional 4,000 to 6,000 jobs for those coming on to the job market. I am not referring to those natives who have lost their jobs for some reason or those who have only been able to obtain one or two month jobs through LIP and LEAP. This is considered a man year, if they are all added together. These are the types of jobs which must be created.
If we build an economic development type plant, it may cost from about $30,000 to $60,000 fo create one job. We are looking at many millions of dollars which would have to be spent to meet the needs of the young people coming on the market. It is a challenge for members of parliament and the House of Commons.
Returning to the report on Indian conditions, the estimated net increase in the Indian working population in the next ten years indicates that between 50,000 and 60,000 people will be coming on the job market. That is a great many people. And when I look at the reserves in my riding, I see that almost two-thirds of those people are under the age of 20, which shows the great baby boom which is taking place in those areas, probably because the job-creation program has not dealt with this problem, nor have our social programs.
How could this bill deal with that problem? As I mentioned before, if we want to meet the technology and the advances in job creation in Canada, there has to be education. One must have a basic education before dealing with the kinds of jobs which are available. The record with regard to native people achieving high school standard is abysmal. Thus, when one considers retraining these people, one finds they do not have a basic level of literacy. The bill does not deal with this problem. A new type of innovative program must be established to deal with this situation. This is why I suspect on-the-job training could be an important tool, since in many cases literacy would not be a factor in learning such trades as carpentry or construction work which a great many native people would find attractive.
Another problem with the bill before us is that it lacks provisions which would make it relevant to Indians living on reserves. We tend to forget that most status Indians live on reserves which are away from population centres. On-the-job training programs are situated in population centres. The kind
of assistance which is offered in the reimbursement of living expenses is not adequate to allow these people to move into the cities. There is a natural feeling among native people that they do not wish to move to large cities since they are not comfortable there. Surely we should deal with this problem. Perhaps some on-the-job programs could be mobilized and moved to areas of high unemployment. Some kind of mobile on-the-job training programs could be set up when a company is building in the vicinity of a reserve. Surely this is the time to set up these kinds of programs which would create employment. Yet this bill does not deal with that aspect, nor does it deal with the problem which is very important when it comes to addressing unemployment in this country.
Another problem which has been mentioned before deals with the co-operation of the provinces. Some hon. members who have spoken before have said that there has not been any consultation with the provinces and that they hope that when the bill is passed it will meet some of the requirements of provincial governments. Most of the provinces are not dealing with the native unemployment problem. Because of our history, it has become a federal problem. If we are to deal with it then we must consult with the provinces to see if the kinds of jobs being created fit in with what the province is doing. This should be an important and crucial aspect of the bill, yet it is not dealt with at all.
I mentioned earlier the tremendous growth of our Indian population. We have had a difficult time coming to terms with the problems faced by Indians who move off the reserves. Employment is the major obstacle. When you live on the reserve and want to work but have no skills, you must move to the city to try to find a job. You cannot find a job if you are not skilled. Thus, you are left in the position of not being able to deal with the essentials of life-housing, food and clothing. Many social problems arise as a result of this situation. When we look at our jails, we see that over 50 per cent of them are inhabited by native Canadians. That is a problem which must also be addressed. Our adult training programs in city centres must address native Canadians who have moved to that area out of desperation. At the present time they are receiving no assistance. I hope these problems will be dealt with by the task force and that when it reports we can add points to this bill to overcome these difficulties.
I want to mention an excellent study which was done by Albert Cameron, who is principal of the Saskatchewan Indian Community College in Prince Albert. He made some recommendations which I hope will be dealt with by the task force and which I hoped would have been placed in this bill. In his recommendations he stated the following:
The training should take account of the unique cultural and learning styles of Indians (e.g. courses must be flexible enough to accommodate different levels of education of the Indian students).
The government should locate training facilities at or close to the reserves to allow adult participation and to eliminate relocation and its attendant problems.
When the above is not possible, the government should set up a mobile training program for trade training, with complete facilities to circumvent the relocation problem.

I think these are three excellent proposals which should be considered. I hope the task force looks at them very seriously.
I want to conclude this portion of my speech by saying that when the government deals with this problem, it not only assists the native people of our nation but assists all Canadians. We cannot continue to shovel this under the rug, because the situation will just get worse. The statistics I have just enunciated prove that.
In conclusion I want to say that I have a difficulty in my own constituency with a pipeline company which needed trained individuals. It was unable to find any place in Canada where people could be trained as service technicians, so it had to send them to Houston, Texas for that training. Of course, the company received no assistance to do that. In effect, this meant training citizens of Canada to work in Canada. But not having the training facilities here, the company had to send them out of Canada where they could receive the necessary instruction. This problem is being addressed in this bill, Mr. Speaker, and I appreciate that very much. I know that while it will not assist the company which I have mentioned, since they have already spent their money, it will certainly assist it in the future if it must train new service technicians outside the country. That is one of the better aspects of the bill.
I want to summarize by saying how important I think it is to use the services of the parliamentary task force, to wait for its advice and to pay attention to what it has to say.
