speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: ADULT OCCUPATIONAL TRAINING ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure to rise in the House tonight, with this assembled multitude, to speak for a few moments to such a distinguished group of hon. members-

subtopic: ADULT OCCUPATIONAL TRAINING ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: ADULT OCCUPATIONAL TRAINING ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
-about a matter which is extremely important to Canadians. As the minister mentioned, because of the change which is occurring in Canada with respect to our work force and its necessities and requirements for education and training, there is a real challenge for young people in the country in the years ahead.
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
I am very pleased to follow in the debate the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) who made a very thoughtful speech, dwelling, as he did, on matters affecting women and native people for whom he has a particular responsibility in our caucus which he carries out extremely well, marked by a sense of concern and feeling. He raised something during the course of his speech which I think is worthy of comment. He indicated that a task force is presently at work, composed of members of all parties of the House of Commons, with respect to the employment opportunities for Canadians in the eighties. He expressed a concern that somehow or other this bill might be premature because that task force will be reporting within a very short period of time.
Neither the government nor anyone 'else ought to take any steps which would in any way undercut or diminish the work of those very important task forces, initiatives which were begun under the government of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) when he was prime minister engaging the attention of hon. members in particular areas. I think it is important that that does not happen.
As this debate winds down, and we anticipate this bill going to the committee, I hope it will go there with an understanding from the government. If the minister or his parliamentary secretary is here, it would be nice to have a response from him before the night is over, that the bill will go to the committee with the proviso that it is not the last word in adult occupational training. Out of that report which the committee will give at some later date, which I hope is not too long in the future, I hope there will be some consultation and some ideas which could lead to an improvement with respect to this bill because, as hon. members have indicated, it is our intention to support the bill.
Therefore, I hope the bill is not premature. I hope the hon. member for Wetaskiwin is not proven correct in that the government will attempt to do something in advance with respect to this matter which will ignore or render it necessary to bring in some other legislation in this area, because it is important and that task force is important. The whole question of adult retraining is important.
I think the purpose of the bill is clear. Under our current legislation as it stands, it must be apparent to the minister that there is little incentive for employers to enter into apprenticeship programs to provide training for people who want to work in the trades.
The purpose of this bill is to recognize the changing employment characteristics of the community, the changing technology in the world, and to ensure that there is some way in which we can be on the leading or cutting edge of this revolution in training. There is now little incentive for people to enter the apprenticeship program because the fact is that at present it pays almost the same rate as benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act. Therefore, there is not that much incentive. Our purpose is to find some incentive.
When this bill extends the definition of an occupational training course to include courses consisting of more than 52 weeks of full-time instruction which would be approved by the

July 7, 1981
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2 commission, it is a good provision. When it would permit the commission in certain circumstances to waive the requirement that an adult must be out of school for at least 12 months before he can be enrolled in the occupational training course, I think it is a good thing. Some young people are becoming discouraged with the traditional school system. Even though they have pursued one course of study, they may find it unproductive and they should be encouraged, as the government is encouraging them by this program, to enter other training programs. I therefore think this provision is a good one.
The bill will allow the commission to negotiate payments to a province in connection with occupational training courses, on a fixed rate basis or a basis of costs incurred. The minister did not answer my question last night but I presume that it will allow municipal corporations to become beneficiaries for certain trades and occupations, and that training in them could be provided.
The bill provides a tremendous amount of flexibility for payment. I suspect that the minister is correct and as people are trained to work in the manufacturing industries and the resource industries, the need for their skills will grow.
In the area which I have the privilege to represent in this Parliament, employers in the electronics industry say that they cannot find enough trained people. A great number of people apply for jobs but the employers still cannot find enough who are trained. As a result, they advertise offshore, in the United Kingdom or wherever they can get trained workers. It is important that incentives be provided by the Government of Canada. If one believes that the role of government is to provide leadership, and I happen to believe that is the role of government, then there is a place for the government to take leadership. The effect of this will be magnified one hundredfold as we move into the new technological age.
Many of the occupations that young people have gone into in the past are becoming obsolete. For instance, secretaries are becoming obsolete-not completely redundant but in terms of many of the things they do, obsolete. The word processing machine has invaded the office. The computer has invaded the business world. Some people are required to run those things but not as many as in the past. New opportunities can be created but old opportunities are gone. Women are looking for new occupations, and that is a significant change. As wave upon wave of women enter the work force in the years ahead, they will demand educational facilities to equip them for jobs that were never considered available to them in the past.
I think it is absolutely important that there be an element of co-operation in the program as well as flexibility. One of the things that has distinguished a country like Japan or Germany from Canada is the fact that they seem to have a national commitment with respect to both the goals of industry and the goals of government. There appears to be a sense of partnership in all the levels of government, and in Germany in particular there are other levels of government. There is also
the sense of partnership with the business community, with labour on the one hand, employees on the other, and that very important third party, namely, government. That is the kind of joint effort that is needed in Canada.
I hope that as this program develops, we recognize the importance of that joint commitment and the fact that labour, management and government are all part of that one thing, the Canadian industrial, resource, economic complex. All are in it together.
If there was ever an indication of the importance of that sense of togetherness and co-operation, it is in the area that I happen to represent. There are two real growth industries in Canada, in the energy field and in the high technology field. The second one is a very important one in this area.
I do not have to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the trend to government spending restraint at all levels and the decentralization of the federal bureaucracy is of major concern to citizens of the national capital area. It has changed the thinking in this area, the thinking of business people, the thinking of politicians and, most important, it has changed the thinking of young people in the national capital area.
The government-stimulated growth that we took for granted over the years is not going to be with us in the future. The two major political parties of the country have decided that restraint, and one may define it differently from the other, is the order of the day. There will be no more untramelled growth.
In families where young people are looking forward to entering the work force, they find that the ranks of government have closed. Man years not used, are not filled. There is a view that it is important to preserve the positions of serving public servants.
Governments themselves are involved in retraining programs. As programs change and government initiatives change, public servants can be moved from one area to another within the public service. That means, however, that opportunities for people outside the public service have diminished. The trend of untrammelled growth and untrammelled opportunity is at an end, however. Even without this change which would have taken place in any event, forces are at work, aside from the predetermined decentralization, that are decentralizing the workplace.
I refer to advances in communications technology; the trend toward office automation; the advent of electronic mail and distributed data processing. All these are leading us to an era of a distributed workplace. All this is having a direct impact on this local area and, I dare say, on the areas of other members.
In the recent past, alternate sources of employment were not easy to find. This was traditionally a lumbering area rather than a manufacturing area, but that business has died out. There was once a very marked and strong forest products industry here and that has decreased as well. Over the past ten years, for some reason or other, another industry has developed. A high technology industry has developed in this part of
July 7, 1981

Canada which I think foreshadows at least the potential for tremendous growth. It began in the 1960s with the establishment of Bell-Northern Research Limited on the western outskirts of the city, in what was then the township of Nepean and is now the city of Nepean. Outside of government, it is the largest high technology employer in the area with a local work force of about 2,000 people. There are other firms as well. There is Mitel Corporation in telephone equipment; Digital Equipment of Canada Ltd. which makes mini computers, Gandalf Data Communications which makes digital and telephone equipment, Lumonics which is in the laser business, Leigh Instruments which is in avionics and Computing Devices Co. which makes electronics systems. There are many others in the service sector and computer business as well-software houses and consulting firms. All have grown out of the high technology industry.
It is the managers, the owners, the directors and the employees of those organizations who are telling us that they cannot get enough trained people. I think there is a challenge here that may affect other parts of Canada and other industries. But perhaps in the same way there is a challenge for business and governments at the provincial and the federal level to all come together.
Here in Ottawa we have a post-secondary institution in Algonquin College. If we are to meet the needs of our local industries from our own human resources, then the courses of study and the curriculae of that institution and our two universities have to be directed toward creating the solution to that problem. That scenario can be found in community after community across Canada. However, it will take a commitment to develop these courses.
I believe this program properly administered will be helpful in inducing employers and thereby young people who are looking for new challenges, as well as young people out of school looking for their very first challenge, to consider training under such programs. We have to get people into the technological trades which are so important to the development of these industries.
Technological industries are not just important to this area, they are important to the whole country. As I said at the outset, they are one of the two growth industries in Canada. With the proper amount of strategic planning, with the appropriate steps to encourage the right training programs, coupled with some decent incentives in the areas where we are strong, we will be able to contribute to their growth not only for the national good but for the good of our young people's future.
Our technology is the most promising in the world today. The hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) is the chairman of a committee of concerned members on matters of science and the development of it. I invite that committee when we return after our recess to visit the industries I have enumerated to talk with the administrators about the need for trained personnel and how that need is being met. These exciting, innovative companies rely as well on the federal
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2 government for technical support. Perhaps that is the reason why they have settled here.
I am rather pleased with the government of the province of Ontario for the way it has looked to this area. I know that all members in the House of Commons, even those sitting on the other side, regard the government of Ontario as a benevolent and far-seeing government. This part of the province is one of the areas where the government of Ontario would like to see development of a microelectronic development centre, according to statements made. In other words, it is important that we develop and build upon our strengths. It is important as well, when we remember the necessity for trained personnel, that one of the steps in the ladder to building the strengths will, of necessity, be the training and retraining of adults to fill the positions which good fortune and good management have made available, not just here, but throughout the country.
I will not take up much more time except to say that this bill is not the last word. It is the first word. But it is the first word worthy of support. It is recognition by the Government of Canada of the change in the requirements of the nation. I hope that it will not always be a piecemeal operation. We should not look at occupational training today without considering the necessity of a large industrial strategy.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) is always talking about bringing forward an industrial strategy. Retraining will be part of that strategy. I would like to see that industrial strategy and where the emphasis is. The problems are immense. The responsibility on government is immense. The burden on Canada as a result of our involvement in GATT, the changes that will occur to our manufacturing complex over the next seven years, along with the necessity to meet those changes, will make the responsibility on government immense.
I do not want anyone to think that this is the last word. It is a small step but an important one in meeting the requirements of our country as we move into the latter part of the twentieth century and the beginning of the twenty-first century. Part of the proposition is that a country is best built on its strengths and not its weaknesses. With respect to that thrust, I say this is a sound beginning.
I want to add that the government should not ignore the findings of the parliamentary committee. It was an initiative taken from the administration of a former government and translated into action by this government in which it asks members of Parliament from all parties to look at employment opportunities in the eighties. This bill is part of the machinery. I hope there will be nothing in the minds of the minister or the government to indicate in any way that the report of that all-party committee will be ignored. This report will likely be unanimous. I hope this bill will be looked at from all points of view when that report is brought down.

subtopic: ADULT OCCUPATIONAL TRAINING ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if still waters run deep, this is a debate which no doubt has gained much attention across the country. This is one of the most important debates we have had in this Parliament. It is not my

July 7, 1981
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2 intention to delay the proceedings tonight. I believe the parliamentary secretary wants to speak, and I encourage him to respond to the points that have been made.
I shall take only a few moments to outline three points concerning this bill. I believe it is, as the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) who preceded me has said, a way in which we look at our own future in Canada with respect to the development of our human resources. Not too many things that we have talked about in this Parliament are as important as the development of the people who are able to respond to the technological challenge that we all face in this changing society.
The hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) made quite a point in his intervention today, and it was also my understanding that the task force on Employment Opportunities for the '80s was about to bring in a report which would have taken a comprehensive look at the employment situation and the problems with respect to adjustment and the strategies necessary to that adjustment, as well as the training consequent to that.
Suddenly we find ourselves with a bill on which we are all in favour. I understand we will give it speedy passage at second reading because we are in favour of it. However, it does not do nearly enough to respond to the challenge of the technological age in which Canada has entered.
First I ask the parliamentary secretary to tell us in clear language why the government felt that it had to proceed with Bill C-67 before the task force report has been presented to the House. I believe that members of Parliament are to be encouraged, as I felt I was encouraged when dealing with the North-South task force report, a subject I will return to in a moment. If we are to be encouraged to take a good, hard, deep, comprehensive look at the problems that have been mandated to us for study, I do not believe that piecemeal legislation is an adequate response.
Second, I have to note with some irony that we are being asked to consider in Bill C-67 measures to help the technological training of people in the new society we have entered. At the same time another aspect of this government is driving out of Canada the very people who are technologically trained. They have been trained by many corporations and companies, particularly oil companies.
I would be remiss in my duty if I did not point out that the so-called energy policies of this government are having a deleterious effect not only on the national economy, but on the human capacity in my province to respond to the technological aids. It is driving people out of the country. It then comes along with piecemeal legislation and says, "Let us do a better job of training". There is a contradiction here in these two points.
I see I have the minister's attention. If he was here a moment ago, let me remind him that I made the point about the use of task forces. Conjoining my first point, I say to him very sincerely: if we are genuinely sincere in our efforts to help
Canadians respond in the development of their own human capacity to plug into a technological society, the government has to speak with one voice and one concern. That would be met by parliamentary support.
I am not going to load on the minister tonight a great big harangue about the energy policy. He has heard plenty about it from my colleagues. I dare say he has heard about it from his own colleagues, probably in more private conversations. Nonetheless, I believe it proper to point out that if the government is serious about training people and helping people to respond to the need to find a place in the new technological society, we have to get together.
I now come to the principal point. I am glad I have the minister's attention. I assure him I will not belabour this point, but I do want him to hear me. One of the reasons that this is piecemeal legislation is that the government does not have an industrial adjustment policy.
I take the minister back to the North-South task force report which was tabled in the House on December 18, 1980, a report of some 38 recommendations. I am sure the minister is familiar with that report. I will focus on one recommendation in the trade section. In my judgment, this was the single most important recommendation in the trade section of the North-South task force report. It had to do with the recommendation that reads as follows:
The task force recommends that the government immediately launch a major public inquiry of the industrial sectors that are likely to be at a long-term competitive disadvantage in relation to developing countries, with a view to adopting effective adjustment measures.
That is a lot of very heavy thinking. The task force said it is necessary for us to eliminate obsolete industrial capacities in our country in such a way as to encourage firms to invest in new and more promising areas or discouraging further investment in declining industries. The report goes on to read:
Assistance given to individual firms should be aimed at improving their efficiency and over-all international competitiveness.
I emphasize that our concern and the long and objective study, and the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras) can attest to this, represented the thinking on all sides of the House. If we are going to be serious in our approach to the North-South question, and that takes us into the areas of finance, development assistance and energy-I leave all that aside for the moment-and in our trade relationships, we have to figure out a way to respond to what in international terms is called the international division of labour.
We now have 250 million people in the world who are unemployed or underemployed. Before the turn of the century, we will have 500 million people unemployed or underemployed. That is not all Canada's responsibility, but it is a subject to which Canada has to respond because these people are in countries that are industrializing and that need to find new markets. If we are going to have some sort of aid program or relationship with North-South, there has to be a quid pro quo. We have to find ways in which we can live together on this planet. One way to do that is not to move adversely against the textile industry in Canada.
July 7, 1981

I hope the minister will not interpret my argument as one that is adverse to the interests of the textile workers. No sane politician in this country will stand up and say we should fire the textile workers. Not at all. The North-South task force emphasized that we are not interested in taking action that would hurt the textile workers who are caught in a situation that is beyond their control. However, it is not beyond the control of the government to phase Canada into a situation through an industrial adjustment strategy that will respond to the needs of Canada to become more technologically oriented in our industrial capacity and to phase out low-level technology, as many countries of the world can fill that void. There is a balance that needs to be attained. The minister is probably quite anxious to see Canada participate in finding a way to achieve that balance.
The task force report certainly was not anything revolutionary. It is not a document that says we have to do something overnight. It stated:
The task force recommends that the government immediately launch a major public inquiry of the industrial sectors that are likely to be at a long-term competitive disadvantage-
Naturally we had the textile industry in mind along with others. What did the government do? It gave a response to the task force report on June 15 during the foreign policy debate which was held for two days in this House. It was the official government response. Responding to that very recommendation, this is what the government said:
The difficulties of the Canadian industrial sectors which are most affected by the competition of developing countries are well known to the government.
The government claims all this is well known.
Measures to help the competitiveness of these Canadian industries in the present international trading environment are already being taken or in the course of being formulated. Public inquiries concerning these industries have recently been conducted by the textile and clothing board and the anti-dumping tribunal. The government will be taking decisions shortly.
In other words, the government is rejecting the recommendation of the task force for a major public inquiry that would last for some time and go into some real detail and depth on industrial adjustment, which we claim to be necessary, saying it has the answers. The government certainly does not have the answers or it would have been bringing forward some comprehensive legislation.
I listened to the minister's speech last night. It was well received in the House. I heard the minister say there were future plans, there is more coming down the line. This is something to get us started. That is why this bill is going to achieve reasonably easy passage. However, I am disappointed, not just personally but on behalf of industrial adjustment in the country, that the government has rejected that principal recommendation of the North-South task force report.
Subsequent to that, a few days after the government gave its official response, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) brought in a new textile policy which, to be proper, was a continuation of the present textile policy, which is a shoring up of a declining industry. He announced that
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
$250 million would be allocated by the government over five years. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) has, of course, a share in this decision, since it is a government decision to put $250 million over five years to establish new employment in communities affected by industrial adjustment, to help displaced workers take advantage of new employment opportunities and to assist the modernization of viable firms in the textile industry. That is what the government is doing.
The people who have been following the government's textile policy and its response to the need for an industrial adjustment strategy that the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton was outlining a moment ago, all those people are very concerned today that the government is continuing to drift its way into this technological future that the minister has been trying to summon us into with Bill C-67.
I feel so strongly about the government's inadequate response to the North-South task force report and the government's announcement of the continuation of the textile policy that I am going to read some excerpts into the record tonight from an editorial from the Winnipeg Free Press. I do not think the minister will reject this out of hand because this is an editorial that appeared on June 23, 1981, under the heading "Propping up Textiles". The reason I am going to read some excerpts from this editorial into the record is that I believe the minister and his officials may very well want to take a good, hard look at the argumentation which has been put forward. Indeed, I would certainly recommend this argumentation to them.
So you will not think, Mr. Speaker, this is a partisan argument I am giving, let me say that I am giving the minister a reflection of what I think is a well-considered, objective view of the government's non-policy on industrial adjustment to which Bill C-67 only opens the door.
Let me quote the editorial as follows:
Five years ago, when the federal government imposed strict and costly quotas on foreign imports of clothing and textiles, Canadians were assured that this was the last chance for the Canadian industry. It was to be given five years to modernize, to become efficient and capable of coping with foreign competition. After that, it was to be forced to stand on its own feet without further government help.
The latest announcement at least abandons the pretence that protection for the industry is temporary. The government will continue the quotas for a further five years. It will provide the industry with $250 million to expand and to modernize. But this time there is no suggestion that, five years down the road, the industry will be any better placed to meet foreign competition than it is today. The clear assumption is that the Canadian textile industry will remain protected and subsidized, to the cost both of Canadian consumers and the people of the Third World, for all time to come.
I interject into my quotation from the Winnipeg Free Press at this moment to review for a minute with the minister the report of the North-South Institute which gave a very detailed report showing how the Canadian consumer is paying about $100 a year extra for clothing because of the protectionist policies the government is continuing. I resume my quotation from the Winnipeg Free Press:

July 7, 1981
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
The textile policy, of course, conflicts with two of the most ballyhooed aspects of the present government's policy-the national industrial strategy and the support of the new world economic order.
The industrial strategy is supposed to encourage a transfer of manpower and resources to the industries of the future. The textile policy, at a cost of a quarter of a billion dollars to the taxpayers and about $100 a year in higher costs for every Canadian family, encourages expansion of an industry which is largely unable to compete on the world scene and which will always pay relatively low wages.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: ADULT OCCUPATIONAL TRAINING ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Order, please. With all due respect to the hon. member I would call to his attention the bill before us which is an act to amend the Adult Occupational Training Act. The hon. member appears to be straying from the subject matter of the bill.

subtopic: ADULT OCCUPATIONAL TRAINING ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
As you know, sir, I never quarrel or argue with the judgments of the Chair. I have great respect, indeed, but I have been trying to advance an argument, that will only take a few more moments, as to why Bill C-67 is not meeting the very objective which it seeks to achieve, that is retraining for industrial adjustment. If you will bear with me, Mr. Speaker, I would ask for your indulgence, and I think I have the minister's attention and only intend to speak for a few more moments, but I think I am putting forth a case for the need for the government to take seriously an industrial adjustment policy that was laid out very clearly in the North-South task force report and which the government in its own response said it was not going to do. I think that is an argument to be presented with respect to Bill C-67. To continue this very short quotation, it reads:
There is an area in which Canadian textiles can compete in world terms and some Winnipeg firms are doing so successfully. But most of the industry survives only because of massive protection and continuing that protection into the indefinite future will only add one more roadblock to the modernization of the Canadian economy.
That, sir, is the modernization of the Canadian economy the minister stood in his place last night and said he wanted. I have said, and my colleagues who have spoken on this bill have said, including the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton and the hon. member for Wetaskiwin, that we are going to support Bill C-67, but we are calling to the attention of the government as surely as we can the inadequacies of Bill C-67 in attempting to meet the very challenge it opens up.
Resuming my quotation from the Winnipeg Free Press, and there is only a little bit more, it reads:
It is particularly ironic that the new quotas should be imposed just a month before Prime Minister Trudeau plays host to the leaders of the world's most economically advanced nations at the Ottawa Summit. Mr. Trudeau plans to lecture the world's leaders on the duty of the rich nations to help the countries of the Third World break out of the cycle of underdevelopment and poverty.
He will no doubt point out to them that fairer terms of trade are every bit as important as aid in achieving that end. He will presumably not point out that Canada's textile policy is the exact opposite of what he is preaching.
We have all said that fairer terms of trade are every bit as important as aid.
The article continues:
Even if he does not, the message may still get through. A week before the Ottawa Summit, a conference in Geneva will begin renegotiation of the international multifibre agreement.
That is also something we paid attention to, sir, in the North-South task force report.
The article continues:
Spokesmen for the textile-exporting nations of the Third World have already served notice that they will go to that meeting seeking better access to the markets of the economically-advanced nations.
I now come to the final paragraph of the Winnipeg Free Press editorial and I ask the minister to take note of this:
They will campaign against the restrictions imposed by the rich countries in North America and Europe against their exports. Canada can expect to come in for its share of criticism. It may be, as Employment Minister Lloyd Axworthy claims, that Canada's quotas are more lenient than those of most other industrialized nations. On the other hand, most of the other nations do not have leaders who continually proclaim their dedication to the interests of the Third World. We are not any worse than the others, just more hypocritical.
That is the end of the quotation and almost the end of the argumentation I wish to present to the House tonight since I said I did not wish to unduly delay the processing of this bill.
I ask you to consider, Mr. Speaker, that if we are to be serious on two counts, first that we are really going to modernize Canadian industry on behalf of Canadians-some very good speeches were made in the course of this debate about how Canadians coming on-stream today are going to have to change their careers two, three and four times in the period of their lifetime because of the speed of technological change today-if we are serious about meeting the needs of Canadians in a rapidly changing, evolving high technology society-my friend from Wetaskiwin pointed out the opening of the third facility in Alberta; we have one in northern Alberta, one in southern Alberta and now there is to be a third one to give technological training because of the demand for high technological skills-and if we are to be serious about responding to the needs of Canadians, we must have a comprehensive industrial adjustment strategy on which to build a continuing training program.
That is the first point I leave with the minister. The second is that if we are to be serious in our response to the North-South dialogue, if we are to be serious in responding to the international division of labour, if we are to be serious that Canada will play a proper role in international development in a world in which we are becoming technologically one society and to which Canada has to respond responsibly with a comprehensive and unified policy for international development where we do not hurt countries to which we are ostensibly giving aid and then refusing to buy products from them so they can industrialize in their own way because we are protecting low-level technological interests in our country, then I ask the minister to think seriously in his capacity to lead the government and this House with policies which will be truly aimed at job creation for Canadians and those people Canadians want to relate to in the interests of a sane world order.

Mr. Speaker, I will not take much of the time of the House because I believe I was able to express my interest in the passage of this bill, and 1 appreciate the comments and good wishes of members opposite in enabling us to bring this to a reasonably speedy and effective conclusion on second reading.
I would just like to say that many of the comments we have heard in this debate have been particularly helpful and useful in setting out the proposals, solutions and ideas about how we can improve the performance of training skills in Canada. I think it also indicates something perhaps far more important and essential, which is that there is an underlying agreement, regardless of party, region or whatever, that this is an objective which must be served by this national government. The improvement of the skills and talents of Canadians to meet the demands of the labour market of the 1980s is something to which there is underlying acceptance and agreement from all members of this House.
While we may differ on the details and the particulars, and while we may have particular tangents we want to follow, it is very gratifying to me to realize as we move forward in this area that we at least enjoy the initial commitment of all members to pull together. Whether we call it an industrial strategy or a labour market strategy, there is a common acceptance of a need to change and reform our institutions of training, education and our efforts at job employment and adjustment so that we can match the skills and aptitudes of Canadians to the jobs of the future.
Many speakers in this debate have indicated they wish this bill had more detail, was broader in its range and comprehension. I, too, wish that, but the timing was not there because we were just not ready for that. Any good idea has a certain gestation period. I believe we are still at the beginning of that process. I hope members of this House will take the time to read the report tabled this afternoon which my department produced, which I believe put forward a lot of new information concerning the changes taking place in Canada's labour markets. It sets forward some ideas which I hope will stimulate their interest and reaction as to how we change policies in unemployment insurance, job training and job creation.
I also look forward, as do other members of this House, to the tabling of the report of the special parliamentary committee which has had a large scale consultation with the Canadian public about the need for changes, and which will provide a very important contribution to an understanding of this very important area. It is my hope, Mr. Speaker, that this will again take place in a short period of time. I want to assure hon. members, because many of them raised the question, that those reports are simply the opening of a debate, the commencement of consultation, and we do not intend to act in this very critical area without some degree of acceptance and accord on the part of trade unions, business organizations, members of Parliament and the provincial governments.
The bill itself is an indication of agreement by provincial governments on the measures in this bill, and that we did
Criminal Code
spend time talking to provincial governments. They do agree with these measures and are looking forward to them because they give us the ability to begin changing our adult occupational training programs. These programs cost the federal government close to $800 million a year, one of the major investments we make in economic and social development. The provinces want extension of the time in which they can provide educational training, they want the ability, when necessary, to sign agreements not only with provincial institutions but with employer groups, trade unions, native organizations and social agencies, which this bill will allow us to do.
So there are very important innovations in this bill which are the first step towards the kinds of changes members have asked for. However, I do want to assure them that this is really only the beginning. There is the old saying that a journey of
1,000	miles begins with a single step. Well, this is one step we are taking in this House tonight. It is certainly my hope that this step will be completed before we adjourn this House this summer, that we will have a complete package of legislation so as not to lose the time to begin putting in place some of the training initiatives required.
While this country goes on to debate many of the major policy changes which will take place over the following year, we can also start working in a practical and expedient way to make changes beginning this summer so we can start training hundreds and thousands of Canadians this fall for new opportunities in the rapidly changing industrial and economic landscape of Canada.
So I thank members for this debate. I hope they will continue to support us in the committee hearings and third reading so we can come forward with a package for which I believe all Canadians will applaud this Parliament because it is an important first step in an area where we all agree action is required.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO SEXUAL OFFENCES AND THE PROTECTION OF YOUNG PERSONS
speechtext:
It is a pleasure to make a few remarks with respect to Bill C-53. As its title indicates, it is an act to amend the Criminal Code in relation to sexual offences and the protection of young persons. The Royal Commission on the Status of Women, the Law Reform Commission of Canada and women's organizations across the country have all levelled criticism at the existing law. Many of these criticisms are justified, and it is hoped that not all but most of them will be met by Bill C-53.
To enhance the protection of children, the bill will create new offences against sexual exploitation of young people by adults and against child pornography. In addition, other changes will assist in prosecuting child abuse cases and cases of abduction of young children in custody disputes.
There are four broad principles I wish to address in this bill. First among them is the protection of the integrity of the person. The importance of this cannot be overstated. It is the very purpose for which men and women form governments and enact laws. The principle simply means that every person in our society is entitled to live free from violence and, as much as possible, free from the fear of violence. This clearly implies that no one should be compelled to engage in sexual activity without his or her consent.
The second principle is the protection of children and special groups. The need for this is obvious. Children clearly require protection from the physical and emotional consequences of activities with which they cannot properly deal.
Third, there is a duty upon government to safeguard public decency. Society has the right to expect laws which protect its members from other individuals and to safeguard its public morals.
The fourth broad principle is also of great importance. It is also properly the subject of increasing attention today, that is, the elimination of sexual discrimination in criminal law. Simple equity demands this. There are many rights of those who are charged, and hopefully they will be enshrined in the Constitution. But hand in hand with the rights of the accused must go the protection of those who are victims. Hopefully this bill will strike a balance in that particular area.
In the area of sexual offences, a number of changes are necessary. Above all, the law must recognize the element of violence. At present rape and indecent assault are listed in the Criminal Code under the part entitled "Sexual Offences, Public Morals and Disorderly Conduct". Bill C-53 would place the new crimes replacing rape and indecent assault in the part of the code dealing with offences against person and reputation. This change would separate violent sexual attacks from the concept of sexual morality. Furthermore-and we have received many submissions on this particular point-the bill would eliminate the stigma attached to terms such as "indecent assault" and "rape". There would be two new offences. The first would be sexual assault and the second would be aggravated sexual assault. Using a weapon or causing serious bodily harm would become aggravated sexual assault.
It would no longer be necessary to prove penetration. That requirement in section 143 of the Criminal Code has caused much anguish and embarrassment to complainants. It has done little, if anything, to protect these victims. Moreover, it has unduly complicated and prolonged trial. Also it has created an anomaly in the law. Some brutal and injurious sexual attacks not involving penetration have been charged, out of necessity, as the lesser offence of indecent assault. The Law Reform Commission of Canada pointed out in its report on sexual offences tabled in Parliament in November 1978:
To retain penetration as a distinct element of one of the offences would be to emphasize the sexual character of the proscribed behaviour rather than to stress the aspect of violence or threatened violence.
I should like to add that most women's organizations in Canada strongly recommend the elimination of this outdated requirement. However, upon conviction the judge will be able to and should consider the nature and degree of violence when sentencing the accused.
Next I should like to deal with the question of consent as it is covered by Bill C-53. The question of consent has always been an essential element in the offence of rape. It would remain a central requirement in the new law of "sexual assault". The bill specifies the following:
No consent is obtained where the complainant submits or does not resist by reason of (a) the application of force; (b) threats or fear of the application of force; (c) fraud; or (d) the exercise of authority.
If an accused claimed that the complainant consented, the jury would have to be told to consider whether or not his claim is reasonable. This is consistent with the Supreme Court decision in the Pappajohn case.
Also the bill deals with spousal immunity. Affected by this definition of consent will be the concept of spousal immunity. At present that immunity prevents a husband from being charged with raping his wife on the basis that marriage entitles him to intercourse with or without consent. This is something I would have thought would have disappeared a hundred years ago. Some concern has been expressed about the difficulty of proving lack of consent to sexual relations between married persons. Some also claim that removing the immunity would involve undue interference in the private lives of married persons.
July 7, 1981

However, proving lack of consent will remain a key factor in all cases where the parties have had prior sexual relationship, married or not. It is strange in this day and age that a person involved in a common law relationship, such as a common law wife, has the right to charge her common law husband with rape. Yet a married person who is separated and awaiting a decree nisi in a divorce action does not have the same right. This immunity from being prosecuted for rape persists. It should be noted that under the present law forced intercourse or assault within marriage can constitute grounds for divorce. There is no evidence in the Divorce Act that this involves an abuse of the law or its process. Consequently, by abolishing spousal immunity the government would eliminate this discrimination against legally married women. Equal protection under the law would be granted to all persons. Married women would be given greater protection of their personal integrity than the law now provides.
The matter of consent is very complex. As the law of rape has developed, so have certain rules of evidence relating to the question of consent. I refer in particular to the evidence concerning the character of the complainant and the doctrine of recent complaint. I will not burden hon. members with the history of these doctrines and laws. I should like to deal with the law as it is today. The judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada in the Forsythe case is a final ruling on procedure whereby an accused may cross-examine a complainant on her previous sexual history and the extent to which the crossexamination may go.
Hon. members will recall that in 1976, Parliament enacted Section 142 of the Criminal Code to restrict this type of questioning of the complainant. As the court pointed out, what we did at the time was to alleviate the trauma, humiliation and embarrassment of the complainant. However, at the same time, the court has ruled that in some cases the accused is still entitled to challenge the character of the complainant by referring to her previous sexual activities with others. In a trial, these questions attempt to blacken the character and are very rarely relevant to the issue at trial.
What is the issue in a rape trial? The issue is: did the accused commit the alleged offence against the complainant beyond a reasonable doubt. I would add that those interested in law reform have objected strongly to this questioning of a complainant's character.
The proposed amendments would clarify Parliament's intent. Simply put, evidence of the complainant's character would only be admissible in exceptional cases. At a closed hearing a judge would have to determine whether the accused had personal knowledge of the complainant's previous sexual character which led him to believe that she consented. That is a very strict and high standard, one which I hope would only be invoked rarely.
Then there is the doctrine of recent complaint. What is the doctrine of recent complaint? I would suggest that it is almost as old as spousal immunity. It goes back to the days when the
Criminal Code
complainant had to raise a hue and cry when she was raped. Failure to complain was held against her. There are many reasons why a woman who has been sexually assaulted would not raise this hue and cry. The foremost reason would be that she would not want to go through a trial, nor would she want people to know. We have looked at the doctrine of recent complaint as an evidenciary rule, and it will be abolished if Bill C-53 is enacted and rightly so.
I wish to make two other points about the proposed changes before moving on to the very important question of protecting children from sexual abuse and exploitation. First, there is the problem of corroboration. The present law requires that the complainant's testimony-and now I am talking about young children-must be corroborated by other evidence before an accused can be convicted. This rule has undergone various statutory changes and is very confusing. Under the proposals before you, Mr. Speaker, corroboration will no longer be required. There is no reason why the law should remain confused in this respect. Sexual offences should be treated the same as other offences.
Second, there is the problem of trial publicity, which is probably one of the most serious problems in sexual, indecent assault and rape cases. At present, in the case of rape or indecent assault, the prosecutor can request the judge to order that the complainant's identity and evidence not be published. Under the proposals before the House now, if a request is made by the prosecution or by the complainant, the court must bar publication of any information which could disclose the identity of the complainant. There is no discretion; once the judge is asked to ban publication he must comply. However, evidence which does not identify the complainant in any way could be published. Along with this provision there is still a discretionary role of the judge to forbid any evidence being published. It is an extra safeguard on what is already in existence.
I would now like to deal with the proposals relating to the protection of children. In February of this year the Minister of Justice announced that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) and he had appointed a committee under the direction of Dr. Robin F. Badgley of the University of Toronto to undertake a very substantial study in the area of sexual abuse and exploitation of children. I might add at this point that further legislation may come before the House after that committee reports. The present law relating to sexual offences against children does not adequately deal with the situation to which young people are exposed. It is characterized by no longer relevant distinctions between the sexes. For instance, there is not equal protection to boys and girls. There are terms like "of previously chaste character", which few judges, let alone lawyers, complainants or prosecutors understand. There is also the term "more to blame", which is difficult to understand. What is done on the "more to blame" test? Are the number of beers which the boy gives the girl tallied up? Or is how much marijuana she smoked taken into account, how much she borrowed, on who went where and did what to whom? It is a very difficult test and I do not know if

July 7, 1981
Criminal Code
this legislation comes to grips with it. I think it is something which the committee will have to look into. We are still into the realm of definition, but possibly at the committee level that particular definition can be restructured and looked at again. But something must be done about it.
It is unnecessary to list the relevant provisions of the Criminal Code concerning sexual offences against children. Rather, I will outline briefly the changes we propose. First, the new law would prohibit any person from engaging in sexual misconduct with a child of either sex who is under the age of 14 years, whether or not there is consent. In other words, the infant cannot give consent. It will not be a defence for the accused to state that he or she believed that at the time the child was over the age of 14 years.
Second, anyone who engages in sexual misconduct with a person between 14 and 16 years of age, regardless of the sex of the complainant, will be guilty of an offence. However, the accused could not be found guilty if he or she was under the age of 16 or was less than three years older than the complainant. The best example I can give, where consent is involved, concerns a girl who is just under 16 years of age while the boy is over 17 but under 18 years of age. The girl could be 15 and the boy 17. In that case, if there is consent then there is no offence. Likewise, an accused would not be convicted if there was an honest belief that the complainant was 16 years of age or more, or if the accused was less responsible than the complainant. Any parent or guardian having lawful care or charge of, or exercising authority over, a person under 16 years of age, engaging in sexual misconduct with such a child, would be guilty of an offence.
As members of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and the House recognized in 1978, sexual exploitation of children for purposes of child pornography is a serious problem. Therefore, a new offence is proposed aimed at stopping sexual exploitation of children under the age of 16. In this bill those who induce, coerce, or agree to use a person of either sex under the age of 16 for purposes of producing visual representations of sexually explicit conduct will be dealt with harshly. This would also include those who print, reproduce, publish, distribute, circulate, sell, offer to sell, receive for sale, advertise, or expose to public view such representations. In other words, anyone who would profit from this filth will be dealt with harshly. Anyone found guilty of any of these acts, or of possessing such material for the purpose of committing any of these acts, would be punished by imprisonment of up to five years. In addition, as is the case at present, the illegal material would be forfeited to the Crown.
[Translation}
I sincerely believe that the proposed legislation with regard to sexual offences would meet the objectives I have just indicated, namely the protection of personal integrity and of children, public decency and even elimination of sexual discrimination. Also, it would clarify and simplify the work of police forces, the courts as well as of juries. I therefore recommend that the House pass Bill C-53 on second reading.

I would like to conclude by urging hon. members to recognize the importance of immediately referring this bill to committee. This will allow for a full discussion by hon. members and for representation by interested groups in Canada which have, for many years, lobbied and presented excellent briefs to make these amendments. I appreciate the interest which the public is taking in these legislative proposals. It is my hope that those who have views to express on them will seize this opportunity to make them known to the committee.

This particular legislation is so important that I think hon. members of this House will understand the intensity of my feeling when I say to the Minister of Justice, wherever he may be and whatever he is doing, that if he thinks so little of this particular bill with amendments to the Criminal

Code, important as they are, that he cannot find time in his schedule to come forward and speak on it at the time it is brought forward on the initial occasion-even though it is late in the night, even though it follows a number of other pieces of legislation which have been brought forward by the government which, in its own wisdom and judgment, considers it to be less important than such bills as the bill dealing with diplomatic immunity, and bills with respect to the measurement of gold in this country-if that is the attitude the minister takes, then I think it is about time that he decided whether he is really interested in his job, and if not, he should turn it over to someone who is, because that has been the history of this particular piece of legislation.
The priority this government has afforded this legislation is now demonstrated by the absence of the minister in this particular debate. What are the circumstances? This matter has been, in fact, under consideration by the government and previous administrations. It is not a completely novel legislative endeavour on the part of this government. The fact of the matter is that while there have been calls on the government to bring forward the legislation for debate on the floor of the House of Commons-and my House leader has raised this matter in the course of House leaders discussions, asking when the matter will come forward-there have always been other matters with respect to government business which seemed to be more appropriate.
Finally, late at night in the dying days of the session, the government sees fit to bring forward this particular bill. I want the people of Canada to know exactly what we face as far as this particular legislation is concerned. What we face is the prospect of going through this kind of limited debate on the floor of the House of Commons and the matter not surfacing again before this session is ended.
After all, as Your Honour well knows, we have now run since April of 1980 a session which originated after the last election. The custom, tradition and expectation is that there will be a new Speech from the Throne and a new session of Parliament in each year. There is now a lot of speculation in the press that by next fall, after the summer recess, the government will consider its priorities, economically, socially and otherwise, and will prepare and present to the House, very early after our return which will take place some time after Thanksgiving according to the government House leader, a new Speech from the Throne. The effect of that will be that all legislation which is on the Order Paper will then be null and void and we will have to start again from scratch. That will be as a consequence of the delay on the part of the government.
In any event, if we get the bill through now, the House will adjourn within a matter of days; I do not know exactly when. The Prime Minister has not indicated that it will be this Friday, but chances are that it will be either this Friday or possibly a few days into the next week.

This bill is the latest development in a full decade of extended discussions about reform of the law relating to sexual offences. It is over ten years since the Royal Commission on the Status of Women suggested changes be made in the law in this area. It is three years-
