Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) spoke from anywhere but the seat of his pants, he might be noticed more often, not only in the House but outside the House. I know that members have been referred to as nobodies 50 yards from Parliament Hill, but the member for Willowdale is a nobody on Parliament Hill.
It is now over three years since the Hon. Ron Basford, when he was minister of justice, introduced Bill C-52 which proposed substantial revisions to the relevant sections of the legislation. It was introduced during the third session of the thirtieth Parliament and was not reintroduced in ensuing sessions.
Under the bill, sexual attacks were to be classified as two offences, indecent assault punishable by a maximum of 14 years imprisonment, and aggravated indecent assault, punishable by a maximum of life imprisonment.
In November, 1978 the Law Reform Commission of Canada made its contribution to the debate on the issue of revising the law relating to sexual offences. In passing, I would point out that a very strange situation arose because of the government's introduction of Bill C-52 in May 1978. The government knew that in 1978, the Law Reform Commission's recommendations were forthcoming. It knew, of course, what the very function
July 7, 1981

of the commission was, and is; that is, to provide advice on questions of reform. Yet the government went ahead and introduced major revisions to the sexual offences provisions in the code only a few months before the commission was to report. That ridiculous turn of events is an interesting footnote to this debate.
The Commission's report recommended that reform be based on three fundamental principles: protecting the integrity of the person, protecting children and special groups, and safeguarding public decency.
It suggested that sexual assault be divided into two new categories, sexual interference and sexual aggression, the latter offence, needless to say, being the more serious of the two.
The commission also dealt with offences relating to sexual activities with children, with persons in positions of dependence. In addition, it made recommendations relating to spousal immunity for rape, soliciting and loitering and wandering in public places.
The government's next move, subsequent to allowing Bill C-52 to die on the order paper, came in the Speech from the Throne in April, 1980, that ancient document of which I spoke at the outset of my remarks. That speech indicated that the serious problem of violence against women would be addressed in amendments to the Criminal Code. As a result of that promise, the Minister of Justice introduced this bill on Janaury 12 of this year.
Bill C-53 is, without question, a very significant and very important piece of legislation. It has become known as the sexual offences bill. It must be borne in mind at the outset, however, that it is more than just a bill relating to sexual offences per se. It covers a wide range of issues. Not only does it concern issues relating to the substantive definition of sexual offences in the code, but it proposes changes in the law of evidence; it deals with the exploitation of young persons for pornographic purposes; it redefines assault; it proposes changes in the law affecting kidnapping, and it deals very briefly with some aspects of prostitution.
The bill has the appearance of being a kind of sausage factory production by the government. It got so far with respect to certain issues in amending the Criminal Code but did not consider some of the important issues that face us today with respect to sexual offences.
One area which my colleagues and I want to address is the absence of a definitive provision in the code or statement by the government about the problem of prostitution. This is an important problem in many areas of our country, particularly urban areas. It has been avoided except for a brief reference.
We must bear in mind the omnibus nature of Bill C-53 because there is more to it than the provisions which deal with sexual offences. Bill C-53 is an important legislative initiative. It deals with some of the more serious crimes in our society. The issue it raises relate to the most intimate and sensitive aspects of human relationships. It must be considered carefully and deliberately by this House and the committee.
Criminal Code
I have a number of comments to make about the legislation and I should like to arrange them in several different groups or categories.
The first area of concern is offences relating to sexual relations with consenting young people. We all know that as it now stands, the Criminal Code defines several offences based on non-consensual sexual contact. Rape and sexual assault are, of course, the two examples of this type of offence that immediately come to mind. There are a number of other offences which deal with sexual relations that are essentially consensual in nature. Most of these offences are concerned with sexual activity involving young persons. There is a rather bewildering array of offences of this kind.
Section 146(1) of the code absolutely prohibits sexual intercourse with a woman under the age of 14. Section 146(2) prohibits sexual intercourse with a female of previously chaste character aged 14 to 16. Under Section 146(2), an accused may be found not guilty if the young woman was "more to blame" than the male for the sexual contact. Section 151 of the code presently makes it an offence to seduce a woman of previously chaste character aged 16 to 18. Section 152 states that it is a criminal offence to seduce a woman under 21 years of age under promise of marriage.
Bill C-53 promises to wipe away these existing categories of offences and to replace them with a much simplified regime.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I shall read two sections of Bill C-53 that it is proposed should, in effect, replace the present code provisions I have just summarized. There is no proper way to analyse these provisions without first looking at them in some detail. The bill contains two sections that deal with sexual exploitation of young persons. On page 3 of the bill section 166, subsection (1) reads:
166.	(1) Every one who engages in or procures sexual misconduct with or by a person who
(a)	is not his spouse, and
(b)	is under the age of fourteen years, is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for ten years.
(2)	No one shall be found guilty of an offence under subsection (1) if he establishes that
(a)	at the time the sexual misconduct took place, he was under fourteen years of age; or
(b)	he is less than three years older than the complainant.
(3)	Where an accused is charged with an offence under subsection (1), it is not a defence to the charge that the complainant consented to the sexual misconduct or that the accused believed at the time the sexual misconduct took place that the complainant was fourteen years of age or more.
Clause 167 reads as follows:
167.	(1) Every one who engages in or procures sexual misconduct with or by a person who
(a)	is not his spouse, and
(b)	is fourteen years of age or more and is under the age of sixteen years, is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for five years.
(2) No one shall be found guilty of an offence under subsection (1) if he establishes that
(a) at the time the sexual misconduct took place he was under sixteen years of age;

July 7, 1981
Criminal Code
(b)	he is less than three years older than the complainant;
(c)	he believed at the time the sexual misconduct took place that the
complainant was sixteen years of age or more; or
(d)	he is less responsible than the complainant for the sexual misconduct that
took place.
There are a number of aspects of those sections that seem clearly meritorious. First, they provide equal protection to both males and females. The code as it now stands reflects nineteenth century attitudes that young women are passive and must be protected from males and that young boys can or should protect themselves. I think we all welcome changes which bring the law into the twentieth century and puts persons of both sexes on an equal footing.
The bill can also be commended, I think, for undertaking to repeal some of the anachronisms that presently haunt the law in this area. I think now of present Section 152 which makes it an offence to seduce a woman under promise of marriage, and Section 154 which prohibits "illicite intercourse" with the captain of a vessel. Again, such provisions reflect the societal values that held sway in the nineteenth century. They are now out of synch with contemporary thinking in Canada and should be modernized. These laws are never enforced, and the rule of law can only suffer if they are allowed to sit on the books.
One can also argue that this bill deserves commendation for the simple reason that it simplifies the law. As my earlier review of the present Criminal Code revealed, there is currently a rather confusing and complex series of offences of which citizens must be aware. Many people argue that simplicity in the law is itself a virtue.
Bill C-53 also abandons the difficult concept of "previously chaste character". For the benefit of the parliamentary secretary 1 point out that "chaste" is spelled c-h-a-s-t-e and not c-h-a-s-e-d. It is a troublesome phrase that is now found in Sections 146(2) and 151 of the code.
In addition, these two sections make some attempt to be sensitive to what might be called the normal sexual activities of teenagers. Such provisions are found in Sections 166(2) and 167(2) as proposed in the bill.
Finally the bill takes what is, in principle, a very sound approach in that it endeavours to protect young persons not simply from sexual intercourse, as is the case with the present code but also to protect them from other forms of sexual interference. The bill prohibits what is termed "sexual misconduct", a term about which I shall have more to say shortly.
On the negative side of the ledger there are some very significant questions and problems that must be addressed concerning new clauses 166 and 167 proposed in the bill. Perhaps the most troublesome aspect of these sections is the use of the term "sexual misconduct," to which I have just referred. Sexual misconduct is a term of imprecision. It carries with it the connotation that there is some sexual activity that is not misconduct. This notion is reinforced if one looks at what would become new Section 168(2). It refers to sexually explicit conduct. It is by no means clear where misconduct begins and conduct ends. Is holding hands sexual misconduct? What
about a kiss, necking or fondling a breast? The criminal law is supposed to be characterized by precision and clear meaning. It is patently unjust to expose people to criminal liability when the nature of that liability cannot be readily determined in advance.
We in this House must look very carefully at the term "sexual misconduct" as it is employed in Bill C-53. We must investigate alternative wordings. The Law Reform Commission for example, defined offences in its report in terms of "touching for a sexual purpose". There are many other possibilities that need to be considered. I know, for example, that one of the reasons proposed by the minister in terms of changes in the Criminal Code involve the fact that the government wanted to get away from imprecision in terms of definition.
In December, 1980 the minister attempted for the first time to table this bill in the House of Commons, and was prevented by lack of unanimous consent, but I will not go further into that. Some other members may have observations to make with respect to the reason why they want to withhold their consent.
On page 13 of the information paper set up by the minister there is a criticism of the imprecision of some of the definitions in the existing code and suggestions that clear definition would be appropriate. There is some concern with the word "indecent". It points out in this paper that "indecent" involves judgments as to what is decent. I suggest to the parliamentary secretary, to members of the government and to the Minister of Justice, whoever he is and wherever he is, that he consider whether the definition of the term "sexual misconduct" should not be more clearly set forth in the Criminal Code.
There are other aspects of those provisions of the bill with which I am now dealing that deserve careful study. For example, certain age groups, and in particular persons aged 16 to 18, would no longer receive any special protection from sexual exploitation. One can argue that in today's society it is not necessary to extend special provisions beyond the age of 16. However, that is certainly a proposition that is open to challenge. We must look at the issue very thoroughly.
Another feature of Sections 166 and 167 that needs thought and investigation is the system of exemptions from liability based on the age of the accused or the age difference between the accused and the other party to the sexual activity.
Under the terms of Section 166, for example, conceivably, a person aged 13 could initiate sexual relations with a person much younger, a young child, and not be subject to any prosecution at all under the provisions of this particular legislation.
While I understand the purpose and purport of the legislation, these provisions must be looked at very thoroughly by the committee. This is not going to be an easy bill to get through. There are a number of provisions which deal with a number of aspects; of sexual offences, other criminal offences and other considerations. The minister decided in his wisdom to bring forward an omnibus bill which includes all of these matters.
July 7, 1981

One of the difficulties is that while there are particular issues to be dealt with, it may have been advisable for the minister, if he had given consideration to this legislation in advance, to divide the bill into separate sections dealing with different subject matters. We could then have dealt with it more expeditiously. That was not his decision. He decided to proceed on the basis of an omnibus bill. Knowing how things operate in this House, I can well understand that there may be something more to it than an interest in getting a bill through.
The penalties provided for in the bill also have to be looked at closely. For example, the sanction provided for a violation of Section 166(1) is ten years. The Law Reform Commission recommended a five-year term for an equivalent office. Under the code as it stands today, the penalty is life imprisonment. It will be necessary to look at the very substantial divergence in those options and to consider what is the appropriate sentence with respect to this offence.
Another aspect of Section 166 that I consider worthy of further discussion concerns the fact that it is an offence of absolute prohibition if a person has sexual relations with another person who is under age 14. It matters not that there was a belief that the young person was over 14. Indeed, under the terms of the bill as it now reads, the young person could consciously mislead the party and still that first party would have no answer to a charge under section 166.
Provisions of strict liability such as this do not sit well with the basic tenets of our criminal law system. People are supposed to be punished, particularly so for serious offences, only when they intended to commit a wrong. Therefore, I would suggest that we look at the Law Reform Commission's proposal that a defence of "reasonable diligence" be available. The accused would be found not guilty when, to use the commission's words, "After the exercise of reasonable diligence, proof of which lies upon him, he believed at the time of the offence the person to be older than the age specified".
Finally, I want to refer to Section 167(2)(c) which does provide for a defence when the accused "believed at the time the sexual misconduct took place that the complainant was 16 years of age or more". I simply point out that the wording used in the subsection leaves the door open to another Pappajohn controversy. The bill does not indicate whether such belief need only be honest or whether it must be honest and reasonably based.
Let me now turn to those parts of Bill C-53 which deal with non-consensual sexual relations, the sexual assault provisions. This is of some particular interest across the country. It is this aspect of the bill that is generating the most press coverage, the most general interest, especially from the women's groups across the country.
There is a very good reason for this concern and interest that has been expressed both publicly and by interest groups across this country. Rape and sexual assault are terrible crimes and are mournfully widespread. It has become a part of our way of life unfortunately that women must at all times take precautions against sexual assaults. They must be careful when at home and when in public. They must be alert and
Criminal Code
wary at all times. Because males do not have to live with what is in many cases a very real blanket of fear, it is a state of affairs that is often overlooked.
Let me quote very briefly from a fact sheet prepared by the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women. The fact sheet, entitled "Rape and Sexual Assault", indicates that in 1979 alone there were 3,388 rapes reported to police in Canada. Studies, by the way, show that only one in every eight rapes is ever reported. The advisory council says that a woman is raped every 29 minutes in Canada and a woman is sexually assaulted every six minutes. The other great issue surrounding the question of sexual assaults is, of course, the treatment that complainants receive at the hands of police and in the courts. Trials are genuine ordeals for complainants. We often hear of rape trials described as proceedings that actually put the complainant herself on trial.
This bill proposes a major and fundamental reformulation of the sexual offences in the Criminal Code. The code at present contains Section 143, the section which defines rape, Section 149, indecent assault on a female and Section 156, indecent assault on a male. There are also sections dealing with bestiality and buggery.
Bill C-53 would replace these sections with a simplified regime composed of two offences; sexual assault and aggravated sexual assault. To accomplish this, the bill would create new Sections 246.1 and 246.2. These would read as follows:
246.1	Every one who commits a sexual assault is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for ten years.
246.2	(1) Every one commits an aggravated sexual assault who
(a)	uses a weapon during or at the time he commits a sexual assault; or
(b)	commits a sexual assault that causes seriously bodily harm.
(2) Everyone who commits an aggravated sexual assault is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for life.
The Minister of Justice states in his information paper that in making these changes "the law would focus on the violent nature of sexual crimes." The orientation of the offence would certainly be changed because of the fact that penetration, an element of rape that must now be proven, would not need to be proven to establish an offence of sexual assault or aggravated sexual assault. Penetration is not a required element of either offence.
However, we must not be too confident that the amendments proposed in this bill will mean that the sexual element of the crime will be ignored. Complainants will still have to explain specific incidents. Penetration and other details of an intimate nature will be highly relevant to the charge. I would expect that largely the same evidence would be led under the proposals contained in this bill. I say this simply as a cautionary note. It is my personal view that it is wise and advisable for the law to recognize that sexual assaults are crimes of violence and that their sexual character is a secondary feature.
There are some aspects of proposed Sections 246.1 and
246.2	that we need to look at closely. First and foremost is the notion of "sexual assault". While the concept of "assault" per se is defined in Clause 18 of the bill, sexual assault is not defined.

Mr. Speaker, the question I wish to raise tonight arises out of the curtailment of air traffic control service at Calgary International Airport effective July 4, between the hours of midnight and 6 a.m. as recorded at page 11133 of Hansard of July 2, 1981.
This curtailment has been caused by a shortage of qualified air traffic controllers in Calgary, which is in turn part of a
July 7, 1981

much larger problem, namely a very serious and critical shortage of air traffic controllers throughout Canada. Dealing specifically with the Calgary Internationl situation, there can be no doubt that this curtailment of services will cause inconvenience and disrupt traffic. As I am sure you are aware, Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding the negative aspects of the NEP, Calgary is a very dynamic and active city with a lot of air traffic which will be disrupted. More important, it will impair safety. That is a very important question.
Furthermore, it has been pointed out by the Air Traffic Control Association that it could raise some very serious and important legal implications with respect to the people on duty. To summarize what Mr. Robertson, president of the Canadian Air Traffic Control Association, said in a press releas'e dated July 2, he indicated the flight advisory services to be put in place cannot provide for positive separation between aircraft, or aircraft and vehicles on the surface of the airport. This is now provided by air traffic control. Despite the fact the advisory services will be provided by air traffic control supervisory personnel, it still remains only an advisory service. Mr. Robertson was also critical of the fact that although some of the personnel were familiar with the Calgary airport, others were not. In addition, none of those selected have been given training for their advisory duty. In addition to the obvious safety hazards of the proposed operation, he noted there are also serious questions of legal liability for both the individual supervisor involved and the Department of Transport in the event of an incident or accident.
Now, Mr. Speaker, at the time I raised the question I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to kindly confer and consult further with the Calgary Transportation Authority. That authority is indeed a very progressive, responsible and dynamic organization which has done a lot to further the development of aviation services in Calgary, indeed in all of Canada. I hope the parliamentary secretary will give this House tonight an indication of what further consultation and discussions have gone on with that authority in order to resolve this problem because the minister did undertake personally to me that further discussions would take place. It should be noted as well that while there is an over-all shortage and difficulties in staffing control towers with sufficient numbers of qualified personnel, the situation in Calgary is somewhat unique given the high pay scale and other difficulties with respect to the acquisition of adequate personnel. This is a unique situation which should be looked at, perhaps in isolation.
As I said earlier, there is a chronic and very serious shortage of air traffic controllers throughout the country. The Minister of Transport does not agree with the observations of CATCA. I must say that the officials of CATCA have warned the Minister of Transport and Transport Canada on a number of occasions.
In answer to a further question which I directed to the minister on July 3, he indicated:
Adjournment Debate
The problem is not of the magnitude my hon. friend says it is. I observe that he has bought the CATCA figures as to the number of air controllers that are needed.
They are suggesting that we need 250 additional air traffic controllers right now. On May 19, during the appearance of CATCA before the House of Commons Standing Committee on Transport Mr. Robertson, the president, said that there was a serious understaffing problem at Calgary and that a curtailment of services would take place. It is passing strange that the minister would reject that testimony when in fact during the Dubin inquiry on aviation safety in November, 1980, the Department of Transport, in its report to Justice Dubin, drew attention to the serious problem of understaffing in air traffic control services. In the estimation of the Department of Transport, 1,036 additional controllers would be required by 19851986. Also serious problems were designated in Vancouver where there was a shortage of 22 controllers, 12 in Calgary, 15 in Edmonton, 58 in Toronto, 50 in Montreal, 20 in Gander and 75 in other points.
In his response the minister indicated that they are accelerating the process of turning out controllers and that there would be 120 to 150 controllers processed commencing September of this year. This is an improvement over the 50 to 60 per year which are currently being turned out, but it will not be sufficient to meet the demands of 250 at the present time and it will not be sufficient to meet the 1,036 required by 1985-86.
The minister must accept the magnitude of the problem. He must be prepared to act. It is the government's responsibility to provide the financial and human resources to protect and preserve the integrity of the air traffic control system in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with respect to the curtailment of the airport control service at Calgary airport between midnight and 6 a.m., the only traffic movements which are being curtailed are those operating under visual flight rules. Approximately 80 per cent to 85 per cent of flights using the Calgary airport between midnight and 6 a.m. do so under instrument flight rules. For those two to three flights per hour, IFR control service is still available as are advisory and emergency services.
The Calgary Transportation Authority expressed some concern that the Calgary airport could not retain international status if full air traffic control services were not available 24 hours a day. This, however, is not true. For example, Windsor is an international airport designated for regular use by international scheduled air transport, as is Calgary. In the case of Windsor, the tower is closed between 10.45 p.m. and 6.45 a.m.
With respect to the broader question of a national shortage of air traffic controllers, currently the numbers of qualified controllers coupled with on-the-job trainees are in accordance with the number of approved positions. However, at any given site a combination of factors such as illness, training failure rate and availability of overtime staffing may lead to periods when normal control services may no longer be possible. longer term, the predicted shortages of qualified air traffic controllers is a problem which is being addressed on a priority basis.
A realistic estimate of the situation is that approximately 520 controllers will be lost due to attrition over the next five years. In addition, there will be at least 150 new operational air traffic control positions created as a result of increases in traffic and the opening of new traffic control towers across Canada. The new air traffic control training system being put in place later this year is expected to produce between 120 and 150 newly qualified controllers each year.
To restate the situation, for comparison, over the next five years we expect to produce between 600 to 750 controllers to meet an estimated requirement for 670 positions. These figures are intended for planning purposes only. The actual number of controllers trained can be adjusted to some extent to meet the actual needs.
POST OFFICE-TIMING OF PARLIAMENTARY SUMMER RECESS-EFFECT ON POSTAL STRIKE-(A) EFFECT OF STRIKE ON SMALL BUSINESS; (B) ROLE OF POSTMASTER GENERAL

Mr. Speaker, I was thinking about finishing the speech I started earlier today, but in view of the fact that I have another important issue to raise, I will not do that but, rather, I will continue at another time to speak on Bill C-53.
What I wish to talk about tonight is the peculiar attitude- and one can only describe it as peculiar-taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with respect to the question of the postal strike. Any thinking Canadian or legislator in this chamber must have deep concern about the consequences and effects of a postal strike on the average citizen. I am not talking about big business or medium-sized business, but about the average, so-called well-defined little guy who lives in each and every one of our constituencies. I am talking about the pensioner, the person who does not necessarily receive a government cheque, but many of whom rely on the mails for whatever little income they receive from some trust company or some small investment. I am talking about the little businessman. In an area such as mine, in Saskatoon, which is not a large city, and in the surrounding district I represent, substantial inconvenience is caused to those people who rely on the mails by virtue of a postal strike. I raised this matter in the course of question period yesterday. I tried to bring to the Prime Minister's attention some of the serious consequences which will flow as a result of this strike. I called on the government and the Prime Minister to take some action to deal with this strike before the House adjourns, which has been anticipated to be this coming Friday.
Regular mail delivery is an essential service for millions of individual Canadians, particularly for those in remote areas, for the pensioners and small businessmen I referred to. Pensioners who do not live in major urban centres are faced with the prospect of either a long period without income or a long
and difficult trek to a distant town. I suggest that Canada's senior citizens should not be forced to be pawns in the government's game of chess with the Post Office. Those in remote areas lack the same access to couriers as those in major urban centres. They rely heavily on the mails for communication with the rest of Canada.
I pointed out to the Prime Minister, as has been pointed out to him a number of times before, it is estimated that some
1,000	to 1,500 small businesses will go bankrupt for each week the strike continues. The cost to the Canadian economy will be between 6,000 and 9,000 jobs. The Canadian Direct Mailing Association estimates that its members will lose $2.9 million for each day the strike continues. This matter cannot be allowed to continue to drift without some government action. At the moment the two sides are not even talking, which 1 suggest is primarily due to the failure of the Treasury Board to bargain in good faith.
An interesting article appeared in the Toronto Star last weekend in which the labour reporter John Deverell suggested that on the basis of his information an examination of the attitude of the federal government with respect to the postal strike is one which is a kind of scenario situation. The only similar situation I can liken this to is with respect to the infamous cabinet document which dealt with the constitutional strategy which we all remember so vividly. In the case of the postal strike there was a scenario set down as to how the minister and the government could be perceived as being tough, holding the line and curtailing inflation. In other words, the kind of government cynicism toward the consequences which the postal strike will have on the Canadian people, in effect, turns out to be the second prong of its anti-inflation program. I remind the House that the first prong is the high interest rate factor. The second prong is a sort of facade which it is now putting on to be tough on a high profile union which does not have any popularity in Canada. In fact, it is one of the least popular unions in Canada.
However, this is a kind of facade which I suggest the government is putting up. It says, on one hand, "We will not go back to bargaining. We will not take any initiatives with respect to negotiations. We will sit back and let Canadians suffer through a long strike."
On the other hand, it says it will not take any legislative action. It is not going to negotiate. I suggest it is an obligation for the government to legislate. Either the government must return to the bargaining table to bargain in good faith, or it must take action to legislate an end to this strike. I would be most interested in hearing the views of the government as to why-and it cannot be serious-it is going to have this House adjourn without taking some steps with respect to the resolution of this matter. We cannot have Parliament adjourned, the only instrument which can allow the matter to be brought to resolution, until the middle of October, which is the proposed time for the adjournment according to the government House leader. We have a responsibility as legislators here.
July 7, 1981

I will be interested in hearing whether the response of the government is really and truly serious about its determination to cause the people of Canada the suffering that it intends to cause them by sitting back, doing nothing and taking no action either by negotiation or legislation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Serge Joyal (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, allow me to make a correction. I am not Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) but to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston). I listened carefully to the comments of my colleague from Saskatoon West and I also heard the remark of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I would ask him to listen, because I think he could agree on some points. The hon. member for Saskatoon West started out by pointing out the disastrous effects of any strike in the public sector on the underprivileged or on those with fixed income which they receive in the form of pensions or proceeds from income they saved throughout their life. It is true that any strike in the public sector has disastrous effects, and they can be more disastrous in some sectors than in others. Let me simply remind the House that strikes in the hospital sector, to name only one, have even worse consequences than strikes in the postal service. Strikes in the education system are also felt very strongly by parents who see their children lose their school days on playgrounds or other public places. Therefore, no strike in the public sector should be taken lightly by legislators. However, when they recognized the right to strike to employees in the public sector, they did so responsibly in the hope that unions would also use it responsibly. Moreover, any union which must continue to serve the public and to negotiate with public support, especially when trying to negotiate working conditions in the hope that they will be extended to all other sectors of public administration, must also do so with public support. This is why an unmotivated strike, which seems without merit or motive called at first glance to challenge a principle, will not find public support, as we can see once again today in this House. Most opposition spokesmen during Oral Question Period urged the government to put an end to this strike immediately. Last week, the hon. leader of the New Democratic Party, the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broad-bent). asked the government to accept all the recommendations in the conciliation report. However, in 1978. the Union of Postal Workers itself turned down the report of the conciliation committee.
Today the same union criticizes government negotiators for not accepting the conclusions of the conciliation report. The hon. member must know that the conciliation procedure is not the same as the arbitration procedure. A conciliation report can be accepted or refused by one or the other of the parties to the negotiations, and no ill will is alleged in such a case. It happened in 1978 when, by refusing the report of the conciliation committee, the union called for a strike and this Parlia-
Adjournment Debate
ment had to legislate the strikers back to work by introducing Bill C-8. Therefore, at this time, in order to reach an acceptable settlement of this dispute while preserving what we consider as a fundamental principle, that of the right to strike in the public sector, exercised with a sense of responsibility, both parties must come back to negotiation. Government negotiators have accepted a great number of the recommendations contained in the report of the conciliation committee. There is a problem with the number of annual holidays, the number of weeks of leave after five or ten years of continuous service and the increase in shift and week-end premiums. I shall be able to reply to the hon. member for Burnaby if he wants to ask me questions during Oral Question Period.
HEALTH AND WELFARE-STATUS OF ROBERTSHAW STUDY OF CHILD FATALITIES CAUSED BY PARENTAL NEGLECT;

Mr. Speaker, I am speaking tonight to protest the termination of the federal child abuse study. Initiated in 1978, this study has been conducted by lawyer Corinne Robertshaw, who was seconded to the Department of National Health and Welfare for this purpose.
From the beginning of the study, Mrs. Robertshaw has involved leading human service professionals from across Canada who are working in the child abuse neglect area in the discussion of the issues arising from her research. She has conducted this research by means of intensive study of legislation and relevant literature. She has travelled to major treatment centres for observation and interrogation of child abuse teams and for interviewing related personnel. Professionals in the private and in the public sector have been aware of and supportive of her mandate since its inception and have welcomed her visits and her requests for consultation as the first clearly visible federal interest in the most malignant of the nation's growing child welfare problem.
Following two interim discussion papers, each leading to a meeting in Ottawa of all the involved professionals with the resulting transcripts of their deliberations, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), in spite of the overwhelming support expressed by these professionals for the completion of the study, suddenly moved to terminate the child abuse study, thus eliminating the crucial final stage in which Mrs. Robertshaw's findings and the input of the multi-disciplinary groups of professions would have been synthesized by Mrs. Robertshaw.
Out of this was to come a final report with recommendations, the outcome of which the consulting professionals have an understandable considerable investment in terms of time and energy, not to mention the widespread appreciation of Mrs. Robertshaw's research expertise and study methodology, concern for the taxpayer's money and, most important, the hopes that many had about the potential impact of this study on the welfare of Canada's children.

July 7, 1981
Adjournment Debate
On April 21, 1981, the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) questioned the Minister of National Health and Welfare in the House following the initial announcement of the termination of the child abuse study. The minister insisted that the study was in fact complete. In this she misled the House. The papers produced prior to the minister's statement were simply interim papers marked "For discussion only", and not for circulation because of the sensitive nature of some of the material and the tentative aspects of some of the recommendations which Mrs. Robertshaw expected to be modified following group discussion.
On May 29, 1981, Mr. E. M. Murphy, assistant deputy minister of the Policy Planning and Information Branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare, wrote all the professionals with whom Mrs. Robertshaw has been working, requesting that they sign a release to allow the government to distribute the two interim papers and the transcripts from the two Ottawa meetings convened to discuss them. It was obvious to most of the people contacted that the move was a ploy to get them to sanction government publication of the suddenly complete child abuse study, with the equally obvious result that Mrs. Robertshaw would not thus be allowed to write the expected final paper representing a synthesis and resulting conceptual extension of all the previous documents.
Since it is this final paper that represents the pay-off for all the combined efforts, many of those most closely associated with the project refused to sign the requested releases in protest, urging, instead, that Mrs. Robertshaw be allowed to complete the study, which she had indicated she can do in six months' time, working alone.
We in the NDP want to see this study completed. We will not be satisfied with the Badgley report on sexual offences against children, because it only covers one aspect of child abuse, nor will we be satisfied with a half-hearted release of a handful of background papers such as the minister proposes. There must be a revival of government support for the completion of this study and an extension of the life of the child abuse study to completion. Only this can prevent the demise, the extreme abuse and neglect of an exceptionally important and well executed study which is vital to the welfare of Canada's children.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dennis Dawson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, I would like just the same to take this opportunity to clear up somewhat the confusion
about the status of Mrs. Robertshaw's study on some points of the act dealing with child abuse and neglect. The next few minutes will be used to clear up the matter.
As has already been said in this House by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), the department agreed to sponsor that important study in 1978. Under the first contract entered into with the researcher, Mrs. Robertshaw, who was seconded to the Department of National Health and Welfare to undertake that work, the study was to extend over an 18-month period. In May, 1980, or at the end of the initial period, a ten-month extension was granted to the researcher to allow her to go on with her work. At the end of that period, in March 1981, two further extensions were granted, the first one to allow Mrs. Robertshaw to prepare the transcripts of the second national consultation held in March 1981, which had attracted the participation of prominent doctors, lawyers, sociologists and other professionals involved in the problem of child abuse, as was the case during the first consultation held in 1980. The second extension was granted to Mrs. Robertshaw to allow her to pursue the question of publishing the transcripts of proceedings of these two national consultations, since the Department of National Health and Welfare had the intention to publish not only the two discussion papers referred to, but also the proceedings of the national consultations themselves. As it happened, a number of participants in the national consultations declined to have their comments made public, pointing out the confidential nature of the meetings. Quite obviously, the Minister of National Health and Welfare went along with that decision and therefore, at their request, the transcripts of the proceedings will not be made public.
However, as the minister pointed out, the House has already been given the assurance that both discussion papers will be made available to all interested parties as agreed. I have been told by the department that the two documents have been translated and that they will be printed as soon as possible. I understand they will be available soon. I must say to all hon. members who have shown their interest in those documents that they will be given copies of them as soon as they are ready.
As the Minister of National Health and Welfare has already told the House, the Department of National Health and Welfare intends to continue working with the public and private sectors, particularly with the provinces, to find ways of controlling and eventually eliminating the very serious problem of child abuse.
The minister intends to urge her provincial counterparts to renew the efforts which have been made within families which are guilty of such offences, and to draw full benefits from the
July 7, 1981

federal cost-sharing program which is available to them for that purpose.
